title: Harness Lab
blurb: Curated tips and methods that make this Field Brief / EM fleet stronger — Grok bots, Mac CLIs, Obsidian vault, routines, and launch standards. Keep only what we can apply; not generic AI news.

entries.title: overclaim — scores an agent's completion claim against a hidden check it never saw and reports the false-completion rate; in its intervention study a verify prompt and both Stop-hook modes gave no detectable reduction
entries.why: Python 3.11+ CLI with no runtime dependencies (v0.1.0) that labels the claim in a coding agent's own final message (complete, partial, incomplete or none) and scores it against an independent hidden check the agent never saw. It reports the false-completion rate (FCR: of the failed runs, how many said "done"), the false-claim share (of the "done" messages, how many were wrong) and what the agent's own tests showed before it claimed success, and it ships a Claude Code Stop hook that sends the agent back once when it claims success with no passing test run after its last edit, or in audit mode asks for a requirement-by-requirement check. Study 1 (Claude Code 2.1.296, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 at low and high effort, 18 solvable and 5 impossible Python tasks, 184 trials, $28.88): failed solvable runs were reported as done 11 of 14 times, FCR 78.6% [50.0, 100.0], and 11 of 98 "done" messages were wrong; in 10 of the 11 the agent's last test run after its last edit had passed (the 11th was unreadable). Flagging "done" without a passing test after the last edit caught 1 of 11, with 14 false alarms among the 87 correct "done" messages; an LLM judge also caught 1 of 11. Study 2 (Haiku 5.5, 18 solvable tasks; arms control, ask-verify, stop-hook in claim mode and stop-audit; 288 trials, $28.08): FCR 5/6, 6/9, 5/9 and 6/7, paired differences in false-completion incidence against control +1.4, 0.0 and +1.4 percentage points, all p = 1.00; the claim-mode hook blocked 10 of 72 trials, 9 of which passed, and the audit hook blocked all 72 once. "The study found no support for a Stop hook preventing false completions." Fit: under our code-decides-done rule a deterministic check, not the agent's self-report, decides done (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check), and claimcheck's card is the source of our claim-vs-record check, where a done claim must match the session record; proof-of-done's card blocks a tests-pass claim unless the transcript shows the command ran after the last relevant edit and succeeded, close to this repo's claim mode and to the detector that caught 1 of 11 here. overclaim's rate is a way to test whether such a gate changes anything. Caveats, from its Limitations: one agent family, Python tasks only and few failures (14 failed solvable trials in study 1, 31 in study 2), so the README says to read the rates as rough; 6 of the 11 study-1 false completions come from one task whose hidden check contradicts its prompt (without it, FCR 5/6 and a false-claim share of 5.4%); the labels come from LLMs, all Claude models, and the rule classifier was partly tuned on these messages; in study 2 the hook sat in the workspace's .claude/ directory, where the agent could read it; a failed hidden check counts as ground truth, and hidden checks can be wrong too; every number is the author's run, not ours; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-11; README, docs/results.md and docs/hook.md read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: overclaim: how often a coding agent says “done” when the work failed
entries.whatItIs: A small command-line tool that compares an agent's final “done” message with a hidden check the agent never saw. In the author's first study, failed runs on solvable tasks were still reported as done 11 times out of 14.
entries.whyItMatters: Our rule is that a real check, not the agent's word, decides when work is done, and this tool can measure whether such a gate helps. In the author's tests, an end-of-task check gave no detectable reduction; reference only, not installed here.

entries.title: cheat-drill — feeds 39 known agent cheat moves to Claude Code PreToolUse hooks and permission rules, scoring cheats blocked next to legit actions blocked; a typical path-based protected-files hook stops 9 of 39
entries.why: Python 3.8+ CLI with no dependencies (v0.1.0) that feeds 39 ways an agent can weaken its own checks to the PreToolUse command hooks and permission rules it collects from user and project settings: sed -i on a test, --no-verify, core.hooksPath, overwriting a golden file, HUSKY=0, assume-unchanged, base64 | sh and more, in seven categories, among them 13 shell routes to the test and verifier files and 9 ways to skip or disable git hooks. It builds a throwaway fixture repo, runs every matching hook for real with the stdin JSON Claude Code sends, approximates the permission matcher, and scores blocked, ask and got through per category, with false blocks on 15 legit controls reported next to the score; nothing in a scenario is ever executed, and --unattended counts ask as got through. The author's measured configs: no guard 0/39; permission deny rules on tests/CI paths plus --no-verify 10/39; a typical path-based protected-files hook 9/39, with 0 of the 13 shell routes; the reference verifier_guard.py 36/39 with 3 ask, an in-sample number because it was written while looking at these scenarios. On 25 held-out cheat variants and 14 controls written afterwards (scripts/heldout.py), v0.1.0 denies 21/25, asks on 1 and lets 3 through (export HUSKY=0; git commit with the variable set in a separate statement, a Python heredoc that writes a test, GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS setting core.hooksPath), and wrongly denies 1/14 controls (touch tests/test_new.py). Both path-based setups' one legit block is adding a brand-new test file: "Blanket tests/** rules punish the behaviour you want." Fit: Kanon's card (a guard must be able to fail) and agent-receipts' card (flags || true and commits made with --no-verify, after the fact) are in our playbook as #check-can-fail; cheat-drill is the same kind of probe for a hook guard, known cheat moves in and blocked or not out, with false blocks counted too. tamperproof's card describes a guard with a shell allowlist so sed --in-place, node -e, python -c and redirects don't slip through, which still allows new test files: the two weak spots the drill found in both path-based setups. Caveats: only Claude Code's hook protocol for now (Codex and Gemini CLI formats are on its roadmap), so of our seats in AGENTS.md only Claude Code is covered; non-command hooks are listed as skipped and managed settings are not read; permission-rule results approximate Claude Code's matcher, while hook results are exact because the hooks actually ran; the README says a PreToolUse hook is not a sandbox, since shell parsing can always be outrun, and pairs the guard with a hash check of the verifier in CI; "The drill measures any guard; this one is a starting point, not a solved problem"; every score is the author's run, not ours; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-14; README, scripts/heldout.py and cheat_drill/scenarios.py read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.whatItIs: A dependency-free command-line tool that feeds 39 known agent cheat moves, such as editing a test in place or skipping git hooks, to the hooks and permission rules meant to catch them. It scores what is blocked next to legitimate actions wrongly blocked.

entries.title: Harness Wrangler — controlled experiments over coding-agent harness patterns: repeated graded runs per task and variant, a confidence interval on the difference, and a baseline with no room to improve reported as no headroom
entries.why: Rust CLI and desktop app (real runs need Claude Code installed and logged in) that measures whether skills, CLAUDE.md files, hooks, system prompt appends, effort levels and models actually help, by how much, and which parts carry the effect. A pattern is testable when four conditions hold: its effect shows inside one session; the result can be checked by a rule, a test command or a rubric judge; the baseline leaves room, because if the agent already gets the task right without the pattern no variant can show a gain (the report calls this "no headroom"; when every task is saturated, that verdict counts as inconclusive, never as "no effect"); and a run is cheap enough to repeat (the default is five runs per cell, and a comparison needs several tasks). Comparisons are paired by task, with 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals. Graders include test commands, diff size, regex and transcript checks, and a rubric judge whose pairwise comparisons run both orders and count a win only when both agree. wrangler ablate generates leave-one-section-out overlays of a skill or CLAUDE.md to find which sections carry the effect, wrangler trigger-set drafts should-fire and near-miss prompts from a skill's description, a conversation task with a simulated user tests patterns such as asking one question before changing code, and a suite diff on a new model lists patterns that regressed, ones the new model made redundant and ones still earning their keep. For review skills you build the ground truth, fixtures with planted defects and safe-looking decoys, each one verified, and small fixtures saturate: "In one project a plain single pass found every planted defect in fixtures of up to 200 lines, which left a multi-agent review skill nothing to win"; run --baseline-only before paying for the variants. Fit: the three-run-proof-detection-floor card says three runs only catch large regressions and asks for paired comparisons with error bars; agent-evals' card became our replay regression check inside Three-Run Proof, where a replay pass means nothing broke, not that the change is good (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check); recalibrate-or-retire's card asks, when a model in the path changes, whether each rule still earns its place, the question the suite diff answers per pattern. Caveats: no LICENSE file, and GitHub reports no license (the Cargo workspace manifest declares MIT, but no license text ships), so it is pattern only: read and re-implement the idea; copy no file and vendor no code. By its own list, poor fits are skills whose payoff spans sessions (memory, notes), skills that act outside the workspace, and permission and safety behaviour, since runs use bypassPermissions; the 200-line finding is one project's experience; 0 stars, created 2026-10-13; README and Cargo.toml read, not built or run. Any real experiment is model spend and a separate Haiyuan decision. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-perch — one-file stdlib Python supervisor for always-on agents in tmux: frozen means an unchanged screen and a known marker, a known dialog gets its keys instead of a restart, a usage-limit banner only alerts
entries.why: Single-file supervisor (perch.py: Python 3.11+, standard library only, needs tmux), extracted from the watchdog a fleet of always-on Claude Code agents needed on a Raspberry Pi. A one-shot tick run from cron reads agents.toml (cmd, cwd, auto_replies, restart_markers, notice_regex and an optional health_cmd), restarts a dead session, and halts an agent with one alert after 3 restarts in 10 minutes. Its design rules: frozen = unchanged screen AND a known marker, because "Either signal alone misfires: an idle agent at a prompt has an unchanged screen; a working agent shows a marker-like word mid-output"; markers match the last 10 lines after trailing whitespace is removed; interior blank lines count, idle_markers veto stuck_markers, and restart_markers restart at once for prompts nothing can answer, such as arrow-key menus; auto_replies answer a known harness dialog with keys from your config, since a restart would just show it again; notice_regex observes and never acts, so a usage-limit banner is alert only, suppressing consecutive repeats of the same last matching line; a reappearing banner can alert again; health_cmd restarts after 2 consecutive failures, for a hung agent whose screen looks normal (the fleet needed a check that its MCP child process was alive); and the mailbox is a file, not keystroke injection ("Typing into another agent's terminal corrupts whatever it is mid-way through"): a jsonl append under flock with per-reader cursors, so agents must poll, plus an opt-in doorbell that types one fixed line telling an idle agent to read it. Alerts go through your own notify_cmd, with credentials kept out of the config, and the dashboard binds 127.0.0.1 and is read-only unless PERCH_TOKEN is set (a Tailscale login named in PERCH_TS_USER can also skip the token). Fit: grok-tmux-watchdog acts on a stale log (~540s) and resumes the same session (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs); juli-os/agents' pane probes tell awaiting input from still working, and tmux-agent-status reads a status the agent writes itself; perch adds rules for when a screen should and should not cause a restart. A perch restart is tmux kill-session followed by a new session, with no check that the old process exited; our watchdog resume-safety rule resumes a stale run only after the old process is confirmed gone, and until its code goes live the EM checks by hand (confirm-old-process-dead-before-resume's card). Caveats, its own: markers are per-agent config you must know up front, and the strings must be adjusted to your Claude Code version; "liveness is 'session exists', not 'work is progressing'"; alerts have no delivery guarantee or retry; single machine, single tenant, no per-agent CPU or memory limits, and no auth, secrets management or isolation between agents, which share a Unix user; the resource check reads /proc/meminfo, with a Pi's default thresholds; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-05; README, perch.py and docs/case-study.md read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: agent-perch: rules for when an always-on agent should be restarted
entries.whatItIs: A one-file supervisor for always-on agents in terminal sessions. It calls an agent frozen only when the screen is unchanged and a known marker shows, answers known dialogs with set keys instead of restarting, and only alerts on a usage-limit banner.
entries.whyItMatters: Our stall watchdog acts on a stale log, and this adds rules for when a screen should and should not cause a restart. Its restart doesn't check that the old process exited, which our resume rule requires; reference only, not installed.

entries.title: Agentic Vault Skeleton — Obsidian vault template: one AGENTS.md that CLAUDE.md only imports, a three-file map marking what is off limits, a skill catalog read instead of the skills, a cache of the last two sessions
entries.why: Obsidian vault template, part of the author's Digital Brain repos, laid out so that any AI agent can find its way around without reading everything. Its rules: "I write; agents read and enrich": your notes are yours, and agents link them and summarize sources next to them, but never rewrite them. One rules file for every agent: AGENTS.md holds the working rules and CLAUDE.md only imports it (@AGENTS.md), so Claude Code, Codex, Hermes or any other runtime follow the same rules. A map, not a scan: three small files in 0 - System/, me.md (who you are), vault-map.md (each folder's contents and permission; the private folder is off limits, with no read, write, list, index or memory, and every scan starts at a content folder, never at the vault root) and skills-index.md (name, trigger, role). Lazy-loaded skills: "The agent reads the skill catalog, not the skills"; a skill's full instructions load only when a request matches its trigger, and a new capability is one skill folder plus one row. Memory between sessions: the agent reads _cache.md at session start and adds a dated block at the end, then trim_cache.py keeps the 2 most recent sessions and moves older ones to _cache-archive.md, backing both files up first. Privacy is a folder, enforced by a separate repo, vault-privacy-guard, which the README lists as a pre-tool hook that keeps every agent out of the private folder. Fit: our vault AGENTS.md applies to every agent, and install-agent-hooks.sh wires it into the agy, Codex, Kimi and DSH homes and the home and project roots, copies a global CLAUDE.md and installs the shared skills into the DSH, Muse and .agents skill homes (2026-09-15-muse-dsh-vault-skills-hooks). ai-baton's card has the same one-rules-file shape (WORKSPACE.md loaded by every session through a CLAUDE.md import on a clone); the memory loop card's recall step scans the one-line summaries and loads only the files that apply, as the skill catalog does for skills; and agent-docs-lint's unreferenced_agent check asks whether any doc names an agent or skill file, the drift a hand-kept catalog can develop. Caveats: hooks.json is written in plain language, so the session-start read and the session-end write and trim are instructions the agent follows because AGENTS.md says so, not hooks a runtime executes; the privacy guard lives in that separate repo, not fetched here; it is a starter layout (me.md is a template, skills-index.md holds one example row); MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-13; README, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, the 0 - System/ files and trim_cache.py read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: CyrilXBT (@cyrilXBT) — memory loop: write only what is new, one-line summaries first, consolidation deletes, say what recall applied
entries.why: CyrilXBT's article (dated Jul 11, 2026 on the threadnavigator mirror) argues that memory is compression, not a longer transcript, and builds it in four steps. Write: after a session, record only what is not already in the code, the chat history or an existing note, one lesson per file with a one-line summary on top. Consolidate: on a schedule, merge duplicate lessons and delete the ones that turned out wrong or outdated: 'deleted entirely, not archived, deleted'. Recall: at the start, scan the summaries, load only the files that apply, and say so when nothing does. Apply: at the end, name the recalled lesson that changed the work, or confirm none did; a lesson that keeps going unused means its summary or the search needs fixing. Fit: the vault and each agent's own memory get the same loop inside the existing daily consolidation, with no new routine; the post-task note template gains a summary line, a 'New?' line and a 'Recalled lessons applied' line, and the done receipt gains that last line. Caveats: our standing rule allows deletions only after Haiyuan's explicit approval of the specific items, so consolidation merges duplicates directly but puts wrong or outdated lessons, an agent's private memory included, on a named prune list; approved items are deleted, not archived, and Decision notes are preserved; the article is written around one model but says the protocol is not built-in model behavior, so every model in the path must be told it; its prompts, weekly cadence, monthly audit and per-project folders are the author's process, not measured here, and only the four rules were taken. In playbook (2026-10-13, Haiyuan-approved) §4: https://caohy1988.github.io/research/harness/#memory-loop.
keeps: write only what is new: check the code, the chat or PR thread and existing notes first; update or cite instead of restating
one-line summary on top of every new note; recall scans the summaries first and opens only the notes that apply

consolidation merges duplicates directly; wrong or outdated lessons, private memory included, go on a named prune list, and only items Haiyuan approves are deleted, not archived (direct deletion only for agent-owned scratch; Decision notes preserved)
say 'nothing applies' at recall; the post-task note and done receipt name the recalled lesson that changed the work, or 'none applied'
skippedAsCovered: per-project memory folders (covered: five buckets + shared-memory admission rule)
weekly consolidation cadence (folded into the existing daily consolidation; no new routine)
monthly memory-value audit (not adopted: a new standing cost)
verify a lesson before writing it (covered: claim vs record, code decides done)
tell a newly switched model the protocol (covered: AGENTS.md is wired into every CLI home by install-agent-hooks.sh)
entries.plainTitle: A four-step memory loop: write, consolidate, recall, apply
entries.whatItIs: An article arguing that agent memory should be short lessons, not longer transcripts: write only what is new with a one-line summary on top, merge or delete stale lessons, load only what applies, and say which lesson changed the work.
entries.whyItMatters: We took its four rules into the daily consolidation we already run, with no new routine, and notes and done receipts now say which recalled lesson was applied. Deleting a lesson still needs Haiyuan's approval of the specific items.

entries.title: workflow-script-harness — test harness that runs a Claude Code Workflow-tool script unmodified under node:test, with scripted per-label agent responses, a counter trace for proving overlap and named sandbox errors
entries.why: Node test harness (Node 18+; the whole implementation is one file, src/harness.js, with zero runtime dependencies) for scripts written against Claude Code's Dynamic Workflows feature, the Workflow tool's DSL (agent(), pipeline(), parallel(), phase(), log(), args, budget). It reproduces that sandbox in Node's built-in vm module, so a script runs unmodified under node:test with no real Claude Code session, no real agents and no network. agentResponses scripts agent() per label, in call order: { type: 'null' } resolves to null to simulate a failed or empty agent call, and a label whose responses run out raises a clear error. budget takes a total and an ordered spentSequence that each budget.spent() call consumes, so budget-aware branches are testable too. parallel() runs its tasks concurrently with Promise.all, and pipeline() lets independent items overlap across stages while a given item's stage 2 never starts before its own stage 1 finished; result.trace records monotonic counters, not timestamps, so a test checks overlap with a.startCounter < b.endCounter && b.startCounter < a.endCounter, with no wall-clock flakiness. Date, Math, require, process and other host or non-deterministic primitives are blocked with a named FORBIDDEN_PRIMITIVE error when called or when their properties are read, and calling an unknown global or reading its properties throws UNKNOWN_GLOBAL; in both cases, capturing an untouched reference inside a returned object can succeed. A HarnessError (a test or config problem: fix the test) is always distinguishable by .name from a ScriptError (the script's own bug, such as a TypeError: fix the script). Fit: harness-mocks' claude-mock stands in for the claude binary and agent-evals records model calls once and replays them offline; this stands in for the agents a Workflow-tool script calls. Its FAQ still asks for a final real run before a script is trusted in production, close to how our replay regression check sits inside Three-Run Proof, where live Three-Run Proof stays the bar (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check). Caveats: the sandbox semantics are a point-in-time snapshot that the README dates as last verified against the Workflow tool on 2026-09-09; allowed globals or concurrency behaviour can change at any time, and the README asks for an issue naming your Claude Code version if they drift; the harness is not a security boundary (Node's vm is not hardened against a malicious script), which the README says is fine because the script under test is yours; it targets Claude Code's Workflow tool, so it applies only where a Claude Code seat runs such scripts; the author built it to test their own Workflow-tool scripts, with no formal support commitment; npm package, MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-09; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: The Docket — Claude Code plugin: a ledger of numbered rulings, a pre-edit hook that prints the rulings cited within twenty lines, and a judge at the stop that can block it on a FAIL or STALE verdict
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (v0.1.0; needs Node 20+, git and the claude CLI) that keeps a repository's decisions from being undone, built around a ledger the agent doing the work (the README's maker) cannot walk past. A ledger is a Markdown file of numbered rulings (docs/DECISIONS.md, or your own), each with the principle it was resolved against, its reason and what it does to earlier rulings, an edge named by one of a fixed list of verbs: a later ruling supersedes an earlier one, often a single clause of it, and never edits it away. Before an edit, a hook prints the rulings cited within twenty lines of it, nearest first, with the edges among them; it informs and never blocks. At the stop, if the session's diff touches a governed file (one that cites a ruling), a ledger or a spec beside one, the hook starts a judge: a headless session of its own, allowed to read files and run the docket's core, which records its verdict. The judge scores the diff against the rulings and its domain packs, and a FAIL, or a STALE for a ruling whose reason the diff has made untrue, blocks the stop with located failures: FAIL directs the maker to change the code or supersede the ruling through /rule; STALE directs it to a dated addendum through /rule. /rule asks five questions, refuses a vague answer and writes nothing until you type confirm in a turn of your own. The witness that checks the rulings is a node script your repository owns and your CI runs, so they still govern after the plugin is uninstalled. Measured results are dated ledger records; the latest judge record (2026-10-02, Claude Code 2.1.287) printed "every outcome: met" over six scenarios, each judge ending 23 to 35 seconds after it started. Fit: our standing rules are dated Maps/Decisions/ locks behind one-line AGENTS.md pointers, and a later lock can narrow part of an earlier one (AGENTS.md's Jev pre-launch step cites 2026-09-24-jev-fleet-shadow-token-gate with § Q8 of 2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook); the Docket keeps that shape inside a code repository and adds a judge of the diff. wordcell's card calls its path-scoped context the missing retrieval bridge between our Decisions/forbidden.md and the file under edit, the job the Docket's pre-edit hook does for a repository's own rulings. Caveats, from its Known Limits: the maker's session may run the core and record a verdict, so the boundary is permission and visibility, not cryptography; the judge is a model reading prose that most likely shares the maker's model and its blind spots; the stale reading is the weakest, met in 1 of 2 further runs; each governed stop costs a headless session on your account, with at most 5 judged blocks per session between passes and the judge bounded at 700 seconds; every measurement ran on one host, and no measurement of the hook has had a control; 0 stars, created 2026-09-11, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: The Docket: a ledger of numbered rulings that a judge checks changes against

entries.title: prove-it-done — agent skill for receipt-gated completion: one-line receipts a bundled verifier re-runs, self-reports recorded but never counted, and two confirmations through one instrument counted as one
entries.why: Agent skill (SKILL.md plus scripts/verify_receipts.py, which needs Python 3.9 or later and nothing else) that puts a small, mechanical step between the work and the word done. A receipt is a one-line check, written in a Markdown ledger, that the bundled verifier re-runs against the real system and judges PASS or FAIL. Receipt kinds: cmd: (no shell), sh: (shell, off unless --allow-shell is given), file: (exists, SHA-256), dir:, http: (status, body text), commit: (exists, touches a path, on a branch) and said: (a recorded self-report, never counted). Six rules: a self-report is a claim, not evidence; a confirmation names its instrument, and two through the same instrument count as one; a config check is not a behaviour check; a check that errors proves nothing; a check must come after the last change; reopen, never delete, so a done step whose receipt fails is reopened with strike-through, not deleted. In the README's example, run with --min-instruments 2, a deploy tool's "ok: rollout started" prints as CLAIM and does not count, while an http: receipt and a cmd: receipt through kubectl pass, so the step is PROVEN through 2 instruments. Install is a copy into the skills folder of Claude Code or any runtime that loads SKILL.md skills. Fit: our done receipt's VERIFIED lists only checks that ran, with evidence (2026-09-27-0xjmori-harness-receipt-and-disproof-review), and under code decides done a deterministic check (tests, file, commit or live URL) beats an agent self-report (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check); cmd:, file:, commit: and http: receipts cover similar ground as one-liners, and the instrument rule would add a count of independent sources to a VERIFIED line. proof-of-done blocks a tests-pass, build or deploy claim at the stop unless the transcript shows the command ran after the last relevant edit and succeeded, and gatehouse binds evidence to GATES.md oracles; this is a skill the agent follows, not a hook. entries.title: bouncer — Claude Code PreToolUse judgment layer: hard rules and a fast path decide in code before any model call, seven Jev questions judge the middle against a YAML policy, and it ships in observe mode
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (Node 20+, zero runtime dependencies) whose PreToolUse hook asks TypeSafe Jev, a fast judgment model rather than a frontier LLM, seven plain-English questions about a proposed tool call in one call, for about four cents a day per the README; each answer is a probability, and thresholds in a YAML policy you own act on it. Its stated rule is that the edges are code and the judge decides the middle: gate.hard_rules and the gate.fast_path allowlist decide the cases that should never have been a probability before any model is called. The README's evidence: calibration run 7 cleared the bar on all seven questions, yet the question naming the risk scored cat .env at 0.15; in run 8 a correct friction fix removed the coverage a neighbouring question had given a live Stripe key exported on the command line, which fell through to allow, and the second pass, with hard rules in place, caught it. Modes: observe, the default, emits no decision and logs what it would have said ("a classifier you have not personally watched be wrong is not one to hand a veto to"); seatbelt, for --dangerously-skip-permissions sessions, stays silent until a hard rule matches unless you enable a deny threshold yourself, and a deny under that flag was confirmed by a sentinel probe on 2026-09-18; guard and full are for prompted users. bouncer calibrate runs the policy over labelled near-miss pairs and prints a pass/fail row per question against 0.85 accuracy at confidence 0.8 or higher; calibrate --gate produces a six-part candidate/reference report covering accuracy, calibration, polarity, rephrase, injection and latency. Latency is not measured, reversed and rephrased variants are skipped until stamped, and no backend can pass or receive an attestation yet; polarity or injection failures disqualify. Fit: company-in-a-box's card records that our Jev layer already had a guard (pre_tool) gate (2026-09-20-jev-decision-layer); gates such as worth_running run in shadow and never block (2026-09-24-jev-fleet-shadow-token-gate), as observe mode does; and our Jev constant baseline asks a gate to beat the always-majority constant before shadow→active (2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook; archestra's card), a different bar from calibrate's accuracy row. Caveats: its 112 hand-labelled fixtures measure agreement with one person's policy intuitions, not ground truth; it catches mistakes and is not a security boundary; a judged call sends Jev a state (the tool, the command, what its paths mean), and the jev backend reads BOUNCER_TYPESAFE_API_KEY, while jev-belay's card notes our router reaches Jev through OpenRouter; the README gives both nineteen and twenty-two hard rules, so no count is quoted here; 1 star, created 2026-09-18, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: five-second-report — Claude Code and Codex Stop hook that asks for a re-send, by default, at most twice a session, when a change-making turn's final message lacks status sections or has a detected structural violation
entries.why: Stop hook for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (Node 18+, one hooks/report.js file; the README says no dependencies) for running many agents at once, when each turn ends in a wall of prose and you cannot tell which agent is finished, which is stuck and which is waiting on you. When a turn ends, the hook reads the session transcript: a turn that only read things or chatted stays silent, and a turn that changed something should end in up to seven sections, in order, empty ones left out: BROKEN, IN PROGRESS, DONE, DISPATCHED, QUEUED, PENDING, DECISION, with ALL FINISHED when nothing is left open; a PENDING item says what you must do (the README's example: "you: run the deploy script; I have no access to the prod server."). A detected change-making turn without status sections triggers a re-send. Certain structural violations also trigger one, including out-of-order sections and excessive item counts. Missing bold titles can pass unnoticed; preamble, trailing-text and soft-ask warnings accompany another violation rather than independently triggering a re-send. A DECISION section without an AskUserQuestion call in the recognized turn triggers a picker request. It answers with a block decision that does not reject the turn: the agent re-sends the message fixed, so you never see the bad version. It ignores re-sends it triggered itself, remembers each message it already complained about, defaults to firing at most twice per session, configurable through STATUS_FORMAT_MAX_FIRES, and CLAUDE_DISABLE_STATUS_FORMAT=1 turns it off. The hook only enforces the format, so the agent must be told it first: the FORMAT.md text goes in CLAUDE.md or an output style, or AGENTS.md for Codex. Its tests feed it fake Claude Code and Codex transcripts. Fit: Gate Inbox reads the tmux panes to show sessions blocked on you, tmux-agent-status reads each agent's own session state, and overnight-receipts lists what an agent's final message left undone or asked; this puts the who-owes-next answer in the final message itself. Our done receipt (OBJECTIVE / CHANGED / VERIFIED / NOT VERIFIED / RISKS / APPROVAL NEEDED) covers Github PR/job and Manage non-trivial done reports, not each turn (2026-09-27-0xjmori-harness-receipt-and-disproof-review), and oversight-readable-output's trial asks for short controlled-language reports Haiyuan must judge; a DONE section here is shape, not evidence. Caveats: of our seats in AGENTS.md, only Claude Code and Codex are covered; Codex skips an untrusted hook with no warning until it is trusted in /hooks; Context Guard's card notes our fleet runs are mostly one-shot grok-tmux-run jobs, not long interactive chats; 0 stars, created 2026-10-12, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Ranking is worst-first; a digest subcommand writes one file across repos atomically, and --json has a published schema. The repo is a 2026-10-11 rename of dawnlog, the npm name belonging to an unrelated tool. entries.title: agent-chain-doctor — one read-only shell script audits a scheduled agent chain (launchd / cron / systemd + the session script) against 30 silent-stop checks, verdict exposed, guarded or undecidable with the evidence printed
entries.why: A single shell script — no dependencies, no network, no writes, no privileges, running on the stock macOS bash 3.2 — that inspects the chain a scheduled agent runs through (launchd, cron or systemd plus the session script they launch) and returns, for each of 30 checks, exposed, guarded or undecidable (UNKNOWN in the report: a check that measured nothing is UNKNOWN, never GUARDED, and evidence prints under every EXPOSED). Exit 0 means nothing exposed, 1 something exposed, 2 the tool refused to diagnose. The failure shapes come from the author's own chain: a wakeup trigger file emptied by a failing date, a stale lock nothing clears, traps covering EXIT only, a scheduler PATH missing the agent's own binary, a laptop asleep through the window. Extras include extras/startup-watchdog, which kills a run that has printed nothing after N seconds instead of waiting out a multi-hour timeout, plus an MCP server (Python 3 stdlib, stdio, read-only) exposing the same 30 checks as diagnose_scheduled_agent. The honesty contract is stated up front: zero EXPOSED means "these 30 checks found nothing", never "your chain is fine" — the false-negative rate is unknown and, the README says, will stay unknown — and the suite is mutation-tested (30 checks × 2 mutants), with a published account of its own GUARDED line having been wrong twice. Fit: a job that never starts produces no job output, while a local scheduler may leave diagnostic traces; our launch standard pairs stream-json with grok-tmux-watchdog on a ~540s stale log (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs) and vigil's card reports a window nothing tried as missed from outside, while this audits the launch chain before the window, beside loop-orchestrator-tmux-watchdog, confirm-old-process-dead-before-resume and the 2026-09-15-field-brief-miss-watch second line. Caveats: it is not a liveness monitor and cannot tell whether the agent did good work; hosted schedulers are unreadable from the machine, and its missed-run-check only tells you the same hour it skipped; the checks are heuristic; 12 open issues; 0 stars, created 2026-09-13, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: dsh-doc-review — DSH plugin: a per-session activated doc_review tool spawns an isolated sub-agent review with a JSON Schema report, a pre-spawn token cost gate and multi-round convergence tracking
entries.why: DeepSeek Harness plugin (Node.js ≥ 20, host @deepseek-ai/dsh >=0.2.0-rc.1 <0.3.0) that keeps document reviews out of the main session. Since v0.2.0 the doc_review tool is not globally resident: a session must run the /doc-review slash command first, which registers the tool in that session's scope only — idempotent, revoked when the session closes, and a session that never activated gets no schema at all. On a call it spawns an isolated sub-agent session with no external tools by default (web_search and web_fetch only under web_fact_check: true) and reviews the document against four toggleable dimensions — fact, completeness, necessity, format — returning a JSON Schema-constrained report (each issue carries id, dimension, severity, a location containing either a verbatim quote of at least 8 consecutive document characters or a Markdown heading line, claim, evidence and suggestion), an adjudication template and a next_action. A conservative token estimate runs before any spawn: a worst case over 20,000 tokens returns confirmationRequired without spawning, a chain-cumulative projection over 20,000 × max_rounds is blocked again, and one confirmation holds per chain_id. Multi-round chains (default 1 round, hard cap 3) read the archived previous round back, compute a line- and character-level LCS change ratio, align issues across rounds (an unmatched old issue counts as resolved, an unmatched new one as added — the plugin recounts, not the reviewer) and stop on convergence (change ratio under 3.0%, or no high-severity issue and zero recomputed new ones, or the cap). Each round archives document.md, review-report.json and change-log.md under .doc-review/<chain_id>/, with chain-cost.json at the root; tests run under node --test with zero LLM calls and zero network. Fit: our locked doc workflow (2026-09-28-opus-draft-astra-fable-review, 2026-10-06-reviewer-rule-docs-vs-code) runs blind reviews whose commentary should not bloat the drafting session; an isolated sub-agent with a schema-locked report is that shape for the DSH seat, beside portable-dsh-multi-agent-plugin and dsh-cos-verify-handoffs, and the pre-spawn cost gate is the run-limits rule (2026-09-23-0xjmori-run-limits-ladder-retry) inside the tool. Caveats: the README is in Chinese; it depends on the host's subagents spawn provider and degrades to same-session without it; references never fetch URLs; it is built against 0.2.0 preview hosts whose kernel API may change before a stable release; 0 stars, created 2026-10-12, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: clear-resume — Claude Code plugin that saves a plain-text handover (goal, next action, status, decisions, failed attempts) into ~/.clear-resume before /clear or cache expiry and loads it in the fresh session
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (Node ≥ 18 and git; one skill, three hooks, one mod) for pausing a long chat without losing the task. /clear-resume:handover writes a short plain-text handover into ~/.clear-resume — the goal, the next action, where things stand, the decisions made and what already failed — a file you can open, edit, paste into another chat or load on a second machine; after /clear the fresh session loads it automatically. Two opt-ins sit on top: an idle handover (off by default) that acts about 5 minutes before the prompt cache expires, either as a toast or as auto, which has the handover written while the cache is still warm, clears the session and then waits — it does not keep working while you are away; and a relay mod that runs /clear after each save and continues from the handover, stopping when its clears are used up or two continued sessions in a row make no new commit. The README reports these separate measurements: coming back to a 390k-token session after the 60-minute cache expired cost US$1.56 in each of 3 runs, while a warm handover plus a fresh session reading it cost US$0.15–0.17 in total (n=3, both on Sonnet 5.5, 10 Oct 2026), about 9–10× less — with the caveat that the saving exists only if you come back; moving a 390k-token session to Opus cost US$3.13 against US$0.24 via a scripted handover (n=1); and on a 30-item build the relay and native auto-compaction each finished 5 of 6 runs, with the five completed runs in each group averaging 37.4M vs 35.3M tokens. A handover is under 1% of what /clear removes (about 780 vs 102,088 tokens, medians across the author's 104 clears). Fit: our handoff packet v1 (Maps/Contracts/manage-handoffs.md, 2026-09-25-rari-handoff-packet-repro-first-promotion-gate) similarly preserves the objective and decisions, with the note itself kept on disk where another machine can audit it; it sits next to context-guard-token-ceiling-handoff-checkpoints (forces a handoff note past a ceiling) and claude-code-cache-keepalive (cache collapse visible in the transcript), and compaction-stress-lab's card is the measured account of what a summary loses. Caveats: macOS has not been tested by hand — the author daily-drives Windows 11, a Linux clean install was tested by hand, and CI covers all three; the cost figures are the author's own small-n measurements; the cache-expiry timing is an estimate; handovers are local plain text, so keep secrets out of them; 1 star, created 2026-09-19, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-docs-lint — zero-LLM CLI that flags missing file and slash-command targets, listed model or plan names, unreferenced agent or skill files and broken anchors in agent docs
entries.why: Zero-LLM Python CLI that catches drift in agent documentation, designed for AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules, .claude/agents, .claude/skills, .agents/skills and similar repos where docs are the source of truth. Exit 0 means no error findings or --warn-only was used, 1 one or more error findings, 2 a CLI, config or runtime error. entries.title: learn-from-mistakes — an agent labels what went wrong; the lfm CLI counts repeated causes per source, never adding sources together, and flags recommendations citing missing records
entries.why: Node CLI (lfm) plus a bundled agent skill for finding the mistakes coding agents keep repeating in records a fleet already writes, such as a defect log or a pipeline's failed steps. The work is split: your agent reads each record and judges what happened, following the skill, and writes the labels and proposed changes; the CLI does the arithmetic: it merges duplicates, counts each source separately, checks that every recommendation cites real records and lists what was never read. The README's example config pairs a Markdown log (each "- " bullet a record, dated by its ## heading) with a no-mistakes store whose failed steps are opened read-only, gives a cause an optional match that counts typed store rows, and sets repeat to min_incidents 3, min_days 2. Log and store counts are shown side by side and never added, a recommendation citing a record that does not exist is named as a problem, and records nobody labelled are reported as unlabelled, never guessed. Exit 0 ok, 1 a label or proposal has a problem, 2 bad usage or config, 3 the sources hold nothing. It never edits sources, instructions or config, makes no network or model calls, and does not apply the recommended changes or measure whether they worked. Fit: our repeat lesson → proposed skill diff rule drafts a fix instead of another forbidden.md paragraph when the correction is already there twice or more (2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook); lfm adds a spread across days to the count, keeps sources apart and checks that each proposal's evidence resolves. harness-creator mines session history and writes the rules, hooks or skills you approve; lfm only recommends, and its label-then-count step is the one failure-taxonomy's card proposes for our forbidden.md corrections. Caveats: no LICENSE file (GitHub reports none), so treat it as all rights reserved and as pattern only: read and re-implement the idea; copy no file and vendor no code; the README's examples are synthetic (a 13-record defect log, a small no-mistakes store, labels written by following the skill), and its end-to-end tests run the real CLI on synthetic fixtures; needs Node 22.13+; 0 stars, created 2026-10-11; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: compaction-stress-lab — 628 runs on two small models: one compaction kept about 1 in 5 exact tool-printed details on real sessions, and a keep-exact paragraph roughly doubled that
entries.why: Study of what native context compaction in the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs makes coding agents forget, measured at the API layer with two small models, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna: 628 runs across a controlled lab session with 29 facts hidden at known spots (108), 12 recorded SWE-agent sessions (240) and its own API agent fixing 10 SWE-bench Verified bugs in Docker (280). Findings: one compaction keeps about 1 in 5 exact details the tools printed on real sessions (19–20%, against 99–100% with full history); losses compound (GPT-6 Luna 67% → 48% → 30% → 23% over four compactions); summaries keep what was discussed, not what was printed (facts the agent stated 79–91%, facts only in tool output 24–31%); one paragraph of keep-exact instructions, printed in the README, roughly doubled exact recall on real sessions (to 41–48%), though in the live layer it cut steps, not failures; 90–97% of lost values were answered UNKNOWN, yet 7 of 72 rollout plans written after compaction used an outdated value (old DB port, revoked secret, broken release), against 0 of 36 without compaction. Its advice: compact late and rarely, at a task boundary after the agent has stated its results, write exact values to a notes file first, and re-check the source of truth before deploys, rollbacks or secrets. Fit: Context Guard's card notes our fleet runs are mostly one-shot grok-tmux-run jobs, not long interactive chats, so this bears on a seat only where its runs actually compact; there, the notes-file advice sits next to Context Guard's handoff checkpoints and our handoff packet v1, whose artifacts and decisions fields carry paths and decisions already made (2026-09-25-rari-handoff-packet-repro-first-promotion-gate). Caveats: two small models, and the README says larger models compact better (gpt-6.1-sol with instructions kept about 99% in an earlier 10-model run); measured through its own API adapters and agent loop, not inside a coding CLI; live bugs were short (7–15 steps), so compaction was forced early; an AI drafted the real-session questions and code verified them, and the question writer and judge are OpenAI models; code and docs MIT, while inputs/ keep their sources' licenses (CC-BY-4.0 for the recorded sessions); 0 stars, created 2026-10-10; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: @juli-os/agents — tmux session runtime: a swallowed Enter is re-sent, never the text; tmux is resolved despite a gutted PATH; pane probes tell awaiting input from still working
entries.why: Bottom layer of the juli-os ladder: a tmux-based agent session runtime in TypeScript with zero npm dependencies (Node built-ins only, Node ≥ 22.5). Its tmux client confirms delivery: sendTextConfirmed polls for the input box to reset, and a swallowed Enter is re-sent, never the text. A startup-time binary resolver survives GUI-launched processes with a gutted PATH (the homebrew ENOENT class of failure), and a side-effect-free CLI inspector (juli-agents bin) prints which tmux binary it resolved. Provisioning dispatch creates or reuses a session, cold-starts claude, and uses pane probes to tell "awaiting input" from "still working". Self-healing is a snapshot/recover loop, zombie fingerprints and a context gate that auto-compacts on a threshold with a cooldown. It also installs Claude Code Stop, SessionStart and PermissionRequest hooks from a spec so agent events flow back to your service, keeps a markdown skill registry, prefers an ACP executor (protocol-level completion) over tmux async when present, and carries orchestrator and voice-call scaffolding with a staged-plan (discuss → proposed → confirmed) call flow. Fit: our long Mac CLI runs launch through grok-tmux-run in tmux, and grok-tmux-watchdog acts on a stale log (~540s) (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs); a pane read that tells awaiting input from still working would be a second signal there, as tmux-agent-status's card says of a status the agent writes itself, and Gate Inbox also reads the panes, to show sessions blocked on you. agent-quota-tracker's verified poke re-queries the provider rather than trust the poke alone; sendTextConfirmed checks delivery at the input box and retries only the keystroke. Context Guard forces a handoff note past a ceiling; this gate compacts at a threshold and adds a cooldown. Caveats: the dispatch cold-starts claude and the hooks it installs are Claude Code hooks, so for our mixed seats the patterns transfer, not the package; comments and a few operator-facing strings, such as the staged-plan voice prompt contract, are Chinese in this first release; the README gives no threshold or cooldown values; Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-10-09; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: harness-creator — Claude Code plugin that turns repeated corrections in your own sessions into at most 3 proposed rules, hooks or skills a week, through five mostly code-run gates
entries.why: Claude Code plugin that reads your last 7 days of Claude Code sessions (Codex sessions too if you agree), finds repeated corrections, failure loops and repeated instructions, and proposes at most 3 rules, hooks or skills a week, each backed by quotes and session counts. Five gates, most of which run as plain code, not as another prompt, drop signals that were already resolved (G1), counts inflated by a single batch run (G2), issues that appeared only in Codex (G3, moved to a reference section), always-loaded rules with weak support (G4) and anything past the weekly limit of 3 (G5). The judge gets masked excerpts once, through your own claude CLI with no tools or MCP servers and your settings, CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins and hooks off (--restricted --safe-mode --tools ""), from an empty temporary folder. Rules, skills and hooks are written to ~/.claude only after you approve the diff, with a backup and undo; memory, script and agent ideas stay drafts. A rejected signal is not proposed again until it happens twice as often, and the next analysis reports whether an applied harness's signal came back. Fit: our repeat lesson → proposed skill diff rule turns a correction already in forbidden.md twice or more into a drafted fix such as skill text or a CLAUDE.md line (2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook); this mines session history for repeated corrections instead and caps proposals at 3 a week, and SessionLens has a similar follow-up, comparing a finding's frequency before and after its rule is marked Moved. Caveats: without a claude CLI whose --help lists --restricted and --safe-mode it does not judge at all; masked excerpts and a masked list of your existing harness, including up to 200 list lines from MEMORY.md index files, go to that CLI; masking is regular expressions plus word lists, with 13 known misses listed; the Chinese and English correction patterns were checked only against synthetic samples, so the README says to read each candidate yourself for the first two weeks; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-10; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: claim-gate — Claude Code Stop hook that by default blocks, at most once per turn, a reply making a completion, count, absence or universal claim without the evidence its rule asks for
entries.why: Claude Code Stop hook in one standard-library Python file of about 270 lines; it does not judge whether a claim is true, only whether the reply shows how it was made. Five rules, each cleared by a command or a named line: completion ("all done", "tests pass") by a code block, a command or a Verified: line; number (a count or percentage stated as observed) by the command that produced it or a Counted with: line; absence ("nothing uses this") by two pieces of evidence (two commands or file:line citations) or a Searched: block; universal (all, every, none, always or never next to a countable noun) by a counted scope or a Scope: line; correction ("I was wrong" with a new number or cause) by a command, a file:line or a Correction source: line. Plans and questions do not fire, and text in code blocks, inline code and > quotes is ignored. In the default block mode the model is told which evidence to add; on the next stop of that turn Claude Code sets stop_hook_active and the hook passes, so it blocks at most once per turn; warn mode never blocks, and any internal error lets the stop through. 17 tests; each detector was replaced with always-fires and never-fires in turn, and all 10 broken versions turned at least one test red. Fit: a Verified: line is close to the VERIFIED field of our done receipt (only checks that ran, with evidence), and the absence rule sits next to our negative-claims rule; claimcheck, the source of our claim-vs-record rule, and proof-of-done check claims against the session transcript, while this reads only the final reply; the always-fires/never-fires check follows Kanon's K-PRIN-11 (a guard must be able to fail). Caveats: it checks for evidence, not for truth, since a reply can paste a command it never ran; English only and regex based, it misses claims phrased in ways its patterns do not cover and sometimes fires on descriptive sentences; evidence anywhere in the reply counts, so one command clears every number claim in the same reply, even claims it did not produce; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-09; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false. In playbook (2026-10-13, Haiyuan-approved): https://caohy1988.github.io/research/harness/#check-can-fail.
entries.plainTitle: claim-gate: make a reply show evidence for “done”, counts and absences
entries.whatItIs: A hook that runs when the agent stops and looks for evidence behind claims like “all done”, a count, “nothing uses this” or “every”. It doesn't judge truth; by default it blocks at most once per turn and says what evidence to add.
entries.whyItMatters: The part now in our playbook is the rule that a check must be able to fail, which its self-test follows by breaking each detector on purpose. The hook itself is not installed, and it checks for evidence, not truth.

entries.title: tamperproof — Claude Code plugin that blocks agent edits to existing test files, including through shell commands, and runs the tests when the agent stops with uncommitted changes
entries.why: Claude Code plugin of two plain-Node hooks with zero dependencies. PreToolUse on Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and Bash blocks edits and overwrites of existing test files (exit 2, reason shown to the agent) and any shell command that names a test file unless it is a known read-only command or test runner, an allowlist so sed --in-place, node -e, python -c and redirects don't slip through; writing new test files is still allowed. The default protect list also covers snapshots and the places expected values hide (test/resources/, fixtures/, testdata/, golden/), and the config file protects itself. Stop runs the test command when the working tree is dirty (auto-detected for Rust, Go, Node, Python and Swift, or a verify command you set), gives the agent the last 40 lines on failure, and after 3 failed attempts lets the session end and says the tests are failing. In the author's runs on Claude Code (Opus, Sonnet and Haiku), when two tests contradicted each other so no code change could pass, 2 of 6 runs edited a test to force a green check, against 0 of 6 with the plugin, where every run stopped and asked which rule was right; on four fixable bugs 0 of 24 runs touched a test either way; method and raw results are in the repo. 28 node --test tests run the real hooks against a throwaway repo, including every bypass reported so far. Fit: under our code-decides-done rule a deterministic check such as a passing test run decides done, and our claim-vs-record rule (from claimcheck) marks a green run after skipped, deleted, focused or gutted tests SUSPECT; Proof applies similar tamper rules at the stop, while this blocks the edit when it is attempted. Caveats: the README itself says 0 of 6 only bounds the true rate below about 39% (95% one-sided) and 0 of 24 below about 12%; its Stop check runs on a dirty working tree, while a push-required kick of ours must end on a clean tree with HEAD moved (2026-09-05-no-exit-while-waiting), so as the README describes it a seat that commits before stopping is not re-tested; TAMPERPROOF_OFF=1 switches it off for a session; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-10; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: tamperproof: block agent edits to existing test files, even via the shell
entries.whatItIs: A plugin that blocks an agent from editing or overwriting existing test files, including through shell commands, while still allowing new test files. When the agent stops with uncommitted changes, it runs the tests and hands any failures back to the agent.
entries.whyItMatters: Under our rules a real check such as a passing test run decides done, and this blocks tampering when it is attempted. Its stop check runs only on uncommitted changes, so a seat of ours that commits before stopping is not re-tested; reference only.

entries.title: Cliffhanger — Stop and SubagentStop hook that blocks on open items in the agent's own checklist or, with no checklist, an early-stop pattern, unless BLOCKED: or another escape applies
entries.why: Claude Code Stop and SubagentStop hook plus a skill, for a turn that ends with work still owed when, in a headless run or overnight job, nobody is there to type continue. The hook rebuilds the agent's checklist from the transcript (TaskCreate and TaskUpdate, the latest TodoWrite list, or the turn's latest Markdown - [ ] list), and the first matching rule decides: a BLOCKED: or NEEDS-YOU: line, background tasks that will wake the session, plan mode, or 3 automatic continuations already in the user turn (CLIFFHANGER_MAX) allow the stop; open checklist items block it; with no checklist, a named blocker allows it and five early-stop patterns block it, the four from the model vendor's prompting guide plus a report that work was not run or tested. It makes no model calls, uses only the standard library, fails open on an internal error, has an observe mode that never blocks, and logs every decision locally; cliffhanger stats counts caught stops by pattern and allowed stops by reason. In the README's 12-task Sonnet 5.5 benchmark (claude -p, with Bash(pytest *) as the only test permission), 6 baseline runs stopped before a green test run and none did with the blocking hook and skill, at about 4 percent more cost; every early stop followed a refused command (the agent tried python -m pytest, got refused and wrapped up). Fit: agent-delegate rewrites exit 0 to 65 when neither git status nor HEAD moved, and stingray sends its half-done-turn judgements to Jev; this acts at the stop itself, before the run exits, with no model call. Its background-task escape makes it no check on our no-exit-while-waiting rule, written after a claude -p run waited on a background pytest and exited 0 (2026-09-05-no-exit-while-waiting). Caveats: per its FAQ the skill did the work in that benchmark and the hook never had to block; the refused-command advice was added after earlier runs showed the same failure, so it was not a held-out test, and it was one model on one fixture; with every test command allowed neither arm stopped early and the hook plus skill added about 13 percent to cost; Codex, Cursor and OpenCode get AGENTS.md instructions that nothing enforces; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-09-29; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.whyItMatters: It acts at the stop with no model call, but its background-task escape means it is no check on our rule against exiting while waiting on background work. Per its FAQ, the skill, not the hook, did the work in the author's benchmark; reference only.

entries.title: dsh-claude-compat — DSH plugin that reads .claude/ skills, commands, rules, agents and three hook events in place, ranking same-name entries project .claude, DSH-native, ~/.claude
entries.why: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin that carries a project's .claude/ and the user's ~/.claude/ into DSH so both tools share one config: skills become lazy-loaded DSH skills, commands user-invocable skills, agents delegation-shim skills, and rules are prepended once per session as a user-role message in a <system-reminder> envelope; installed Claude Code plugins add their skills, commands and agents at the lowest rank. A hook subset (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit) runs via /bin/sh -c with the Claude-style JSON on stdin: exit 2 denies or blocks, other non-zero exits and timeouts allow with a warning. A project-root .mcp.json becomes dsh-mcp-client instances, and plugin-declared MCP servers mount only with enablePluginMcp (off by default). Same-name skills, commands, rules and agents resolve in a fixed order, project .claude over DSH native over ~/.claude; CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, which it never touches, stay with DSH's built-in dsh-agent-instructions. Fit: our install-agent-hooks.sh wires the vault AGENTS.md into ~/.dsh and installs the shared skills into ~/.dsh/skills, ~/.agents/skills and project .agents and .dsh mirrors (2026-09-15-muse-dsh-vault-skills-hooks), so this would add .claude/ trees under a stated order and leave that AGENTS.md wiring alone; cinch translates one SKILL.md per harness, and catstack and skillwharf link one copy into several. entries.title: dsh-goal-wait-gate — DSH plugin that by default withholds automatic goal continuation while the session still has a running or stopping background job or a live subagent
entries.why: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin for a known, still-unfixed upstream behavior through DSH 0.2.1-alpha.1: the official driver injects a <goal_round> prompt whenever an agent is idle and its goal is active and armed, and idle only means no turn is running, so an agent that ended its turn to wait on a background job or subagent gets goal rounds that use up the round budget and re-prefill the whole session. Live work is a job the session owns in running or stopping status (read from ctx.jobs.list) or a live subagent descendant at any depth. The gate evaluates at agent/turn-stopping, at agent/status idle and on goal/changed; in the default activation strategy, while live work exists and the goal is active and armed, it calls ctx.goals.disarm, then ctx.goals.resume on its own hold once the work has settled and its completion-notice turn has ended. It never calls pause, never resumes a goal it did not disarm, drops its hold on an explicit human re-arm, and re-arms held goals when unloaded. Its bundle layer disables DSH's own goal-round-driver row and mounts the driver itself, so switching the row off means no automatic continuation (the native strategy restores official behavior); maxHoldMs defaults to 0, which holds indefinitely. Fit: the DSH goal-mode side of our no-exit-while-waiting rule (never end a turn waiting on background work and then commit): a DSH agent that does end its turn to wait gets no goal rounds until the work has settled; stingray's unwatched check intercepts the opposite case, a promise to monitor with no background task, session cron or handoff behind it. Caveats: the README lists DSH 0.1.7-alpha.2 through 0.2.0-rc.2 (declared peer range >=0.1.7-alpha.2 <0.3) and Node 22+, and its opt-in startup owner runs only on exactly pinned 0.2.0-rc.2 and 0.2.1-alpha.1 hosts; not on npm; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-24; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: Hold automatic goal prompts while an agent waits on background work

entries.whyItMatters: It fits the goal-mode side of our rule against ending a turn to wait on background work and then committing: an agent that does wait gets no goal prompts until the work settles. Built for pre-release versions; reference only, not installed.

entries.title: jev-belay — Claude Code Stop hook that reads the turn's transcript first and spends one Jev call only when files changed and no check has passed since
entries.why: Claude Code Stop hook (plugin or settings.json hook) for a final message that calls the work done when nothing backs it. It reads the transcript slice since the last prompt locally with two regex belts: a test, build or lint runner named in a command, and a runner's own summary in the output. If nothing changed, or a check passed after the last change, the hook exits and Jev is never asked. Only when something changed and nothing proved it does it send one jev-1.13.0 call with four questions, $0.00005 per call and 346 ms median latency; if the answer is an unverified done, it blocks the stop (exit 2) and Claude is told to run the tests, build or lint and report the actual result. Only the prompt, the closing message and two counts leave the machine. Blocks are capped at one per prompt, none within 60 seconds of the last and three per session; every error path exits 0; a shadow mode only reports what it would have blocked. Measured on 100 labeled stops: AUROC 0.976 against 0.777 for the wording alone, blocking 8 turns in 100, 7 rightly. Fit: it keeps the order of our code-decides-done rule, where a deterministic check outranks Jev's completion_check: a passing check ends the turn with no Jev call, and Jev's answer only decides whether to block; it sits next to proof-of-done (no network or model call) and stingray (half-done stops judged by Jev). Caveats: the corpus is the author's own sessions, labeled by a model rather than by hand, with 12 false dones, so the README puts the AUROC interval at about ±0.06, and only one of its four thresholds (claims_done) was swept; a turn with no file edits never reaches the question; a custom check script is invisible unless named in the check option or its output carries a runner summary the hook knows; it needs Node 20+, Claude Code 2.1.196+ and a TypeSafe key (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), while our router reaches Jev through OpenRouter; headless claude -p behavior not verified here; MIT, 34 stars, created 2026-09-18; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: A stop check that asks a judge model only when no check passed after edits
entries.whatItIs: A hook that runs when the agent stops. If nothing changed, or a test, build or lint run passed after the last change, it lets the stop through; otherwise one call to a judgment model decides whether to block.
entries.whyItMatters: It keeps the order of our rule that a real check outranks the decision layer's completion check: a passing check ends the turn with no model call. On 100 model-labeled stops from the author's own sessions it blocked 8, 7 rightly; reference only.

entries.title: agent-delegate — non-interactive coding-agent harness: exit 0 becomes 65 when neither git status nor HEAD moved, the agent's config header is echoed, stdin is /dev/null
entries.why: Bash harness (delegate.sh, worktree.sh, review-status.sh and a spec template) for handing a written spec to a non-interactive coding agent; it defaults to codex exec, and AGENT_CMD takes any agent that accepts a prompt and a working directory. Five guards, each from an incident: it snapshots git status and HEAD before and after the run and, when neither moved, rewrites exit 0 to 65, so an agent that asked for approval into a run with nobody to answer cannot pass as success (HEAD counts because an agent that commits leaves a clean status); after the run it echoes the agent's own config header lines so a silent effort downgrade shows; it runs the agent with stdin from /dev/null, since a detached agent otherwise blocks on stdin; in a git worktree it grants the shared git dir so commits do not die on index.lock; and it tells callers to use set -o pipefail, because piping its output through tail reports tail's status. Other exits: 64 bad usage, 66 missing project or spec. Its review order starts with whether anything was produced, because tests always pass when nothing changed. Fit: our no-exit-while-waiting wrapper gate fails a push-required kick on a dirty tree or an unchanged HEAD; exit 65 is a looser no-op signal for any run, push or not; and the header echo would show, per run, the reasoning effort to compare with our 2026-09-24 Astra xhigh default. Caveats: the defaults are set for codex exec (-s workspace-write) and pass -c model_reasoning_effort=high, below the xhigh that lock sets for Astra, so our seats would need those overridden; its tests are ten cases driven by stub agents; no network calls except an optional webhook; a pay-what-you-want Gumroad zip adds an installer and support, and the README calls the repo code the whole product; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-22; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: agent-delegate: hand a spec to a coding agent and catch runs that did nothing
entries.whatItIs: A shell harness that hands a written spec to a coding agent with nobody watching. If neither git status nor the latest commit moved, it turns a success exit into a no-change code, and it prints the agent's config header so a quiet effort downgrade shows.
entries.whyItMatters: Our wrapper already fails a push-required run on a dirty tree or unchanged commit; its no-change code is a looser signal for any run, and the header would show each run's effort. Its defaults would need overrides for our seats; reference only.

entries.title: verified-ops-starter — freshness, no-op and rollout checks for scheduled jobs under one exit-code contract in which a dead checker cannot look like a clean result
entries.why: Python standard-library kit that replaces a scheduled job's self-report with evidence. freshness asks whether the job's real output is young enough (optional min_bytes, and a contains marker taken from the body, never the filename); wrap runs the job and announces a silent no-op when it exits 0 but its artifact did not change, comparing mtime and size, and kills and announces a hang under --timeout-s; rollout reads a fix back from each target, and a target whose verify only exits 0 comes back WEAK. One exit contract: 0 clean, 1 a problem found and the alert delivered, 3 found but the alert could not be delivered (also what --dry-run returns), 4 the checker itself died; a run that measured nothing, such as an empty or misspelled config, is 4, never 0, and under wrap any non-zero child code becomes 4 unless declared with --signal. selftest.py runs 44 checks, each first broken by a mutant, under the README's rule that a check with no mutant that makes it fail measures nothing. Fit: that rule is Kanon's K-PRIN-11 (a guard must be able to fail) in runnable form; 4 for nothing measured is Ruttla's exit 2 under another number; and wrap catches a job that exits 0 after an empty page or an expired token, the failure our negative-claims rule says must be a gap, never zero. Caveats: mtime is evidence, not proof (a third process writing the artifact mid-run reads as work landed, and a byte-identical rewrite on a coarse filesystem can read as a no-op), and a synced folder can stamp a fresh mtime on an old file; it answers whether the work landed, not whether the job fired, so the README puts it beside heartbeat monitoring rather than in place of it; Python 3.8+, CI on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows, v0.1.0; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-08-04; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false. entries.plainTitle: verified-ops-starter: check that a scheduled job's work really landed
entries.whatItIs: A small kit that replaces a scheduled job's self-report with evidence: it checks the output is fresh, flags a job that exits cleanly but left its output unchanged, and uses exit codes where a dead checker or one that measured nothing can't look clean.
entries.whyItMatters: The part now in our playbook is the rule that a check must be able to fail, which its self-test puts in runnable form by breaking each check on purpose first. The kit itself is not installed.

entries.title: Vigil — holds a scheduled agent's claim to independent checks you declare, reports a window nothing tried as missed and can re-run it, and flags identical output N runs in a row
entries.why: Python verification layer that supervises a scheduled job from outside and keeps two things apart: the claim, what the job says it did (JSON written to $VIGIL_CLAIM or one stdout line), and the check, evidence from outside the job (a file changed recently or has real content, an endpoint returns 200, a command passes, a metric went up). Verdicts: verified (exited 0 and the checks agree), unverified (exited 0, the evidence does not support it), failed (nonzero exit or timeout), missed (the window closed and nothing even tried), degraded (identical output N runs in a row, set by degrade_after). Schedules are declared in vigil.toml, which is how it can report a run that never happened; vigil catchup re-runs uncovered windows (the README's case: a laptop asleep through its 9:15 window); vigil run exits 0 on verified, 1 on failed and 2 on unverified or degraded; vigil check exits 1 if any job is missed, unverified or degraded. A job can also be watched without a command, checking only the artifact that window should have left. No daemon or database: it runs when the scheduler runs it and keeps one JSON state file; alerts are deduplicated per job. Fit: our Field Brief miss-watch (Collection's :44 catch-up when the :34 brief is missing) is the same missed-window idea for one routine; the README's demo bug, an except that returns an empty list so a dead source looks like a quiet day, is the case our negative-claims rule makes a gap. Caveats: a job with no checks behaves like cron again, and claim_field only checks the claim against itself, so a job that lies in its claim passes it; a watched job proves the artifact exists, not that the run succeeded; vigil.toml runs commands through a shell, so it is trusted input; identical output is also what a job with genuinely unchanged data produces, so degrade_after needs care; Python 3.11+; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-24, last push 2026-10-02; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
