entries.whyItMatters: In playbook: an agent’s word alone does not turn a slot green; the real result is re-checked first.

entries.title: Single-target handoff + hop cap
entries.why: DSH Lab KEEP (OpenBot): only the first @mention in a bot reply wakes another bot; hop cap default 2 then ask Haiyuan — never silent misroute. Rooms also: ack/final discipline (≤1 ack + 1 final).
entries.plainTitle: One handoff target per bot reply, and a cap on bot-to-bot hops
entries.whatItIs: A rule kept from the OpenBot pattern: only the first mention in a bot’s reply wakes another bot, and after 2 hops, the default cap, the bots ask Haiyuan instead of routing on.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook, so work is never silently misrouted; our group rooms also keep to at most one acknowledgment and one final reply.

entries.title: Lab #2 spikes: llmtap / jev-guard / GBDL (backlog)
entries.why: DSH 2026-09-20 backlog only — not installed: llmtap per-seat cost proxy; jev-guard Coding EM smoke; GBDL-shaped vault export of bot defs (convention). Playbook notes under §11 Lab follow-ups.
entries.plainTitle: Three parked spikes: per-seat cost, a guard smoke test, bot exports
entries.whatItIs: Three backlog ideas from one Lab scouting round: llmtap, a proxy that tracks cost per coding seat; a smoke test of a decision-layer guard in the coding loop; and a vault export of bot definitions in a set format, as a convention.
entries.whyItMatters: They point at per-seat spend tracking and keeping bot setups on file. Backlog only and not installed; the playbook lists them under Lab follow-ups.

entries.title: jev-browser Lab backlog (no Playwright)
entries.why: KEEP candidate parked: Playwright + Jev click decisions. Do not install Playwright. pre_browser gate already filters computerUse.
entries.plainTitle: Parked idea: browser clicks decided by our decision layer
entries.whatItIs: A parked candidate: pair a browser automation tool with our decision layer so the layer makes the click decisions.
entries.whyItMatters: Backlog only: the browser tool is not to be installed, and an existing gate before browser actions already filters computer-use requests.

entries.title: Harness engineering: Codex in an agent-first world (OpenAI)
entries.why: Repo/docs as system of record: short indexes, durable specs/plans, decision logs, linted invariants, doc-gardening. Maps onto our EM intent/spec/plan + dual-LGTM and vault Decisions.
entries.plainTitle: Harness engineering: the repo and its docs as the system of record
entries.whatItIs: A model maker’s engineering post on agent-first work: keep the repo and docs as the system of record, with short indexes, lasting specs and plans, decision logs, invariants checked by linters, and regular doc cleanup.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook: these ideas map onto our coding loop of intent, spec and plan with two blind reviews, and onto the decision notes in our vault.

entries.title: How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)
entries.why: Lead plans → fan-out collectors → persist artifacts → synthesize + citation-check. Direct template for Field Brief collect→brief→publish and Manage CoS effort budgets.
entries.plainTitle: “How we built our multi-agent research system”: lead agent plus collectors
entries.whatItIs: A model maker’s engineering post on its research agents: a lead agent plans, fans out to collector agents, saves their artifacts, then synthesizes the results and checks citations.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook as a direct template for our Field Brief (collect, write, publish) and for the effort budgets the manager bot sets as chief of staff.

entries.title: Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions (docs)
entries.why: Lead/teammate, shared task list, messaging, tmux splits, idle/complete hooks — concrete patterns for our group rooms + Mac CLI fleet ops.
entries.plainTitle: Docs on running a team of coding-agent sessions under a lead
entries.whatItIs: Product docs for one coding CLI on running its sessions as a team: a lead and teammates, a shared task list, messaging, split terminal panes, and hooks that run when a session is idle or complete.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook as concrete patterns for our group rooms and for running our fleet of coding agents on the Mac.

entries.title: Watchdog — local operator control plane for agentic loops
entries.why: KEEP optional for Codex/Astra observe (Mac 2026-09-16: observe --once works; doctor still crashes). Do not replace grok-tmux-watchdog fleet-wide.
entries.plainTitle: Watchdog: a local control layer for operating agent loops
entries.whatItIs: A local control plane for operators of agent loops, meaning one place to observe and control them. In our Mac test, its one-shot observe mode worked, but its doctor command still crashed.
entries.whyItMatters: Kept as an optional follow-up for observing one of our coding seats; it should not replace our stall watchdog across the fleet.

entries.title: receipt — itemized AI coding-agent cost on PRs
entries.why: KEEP for Coding EM (Claude import). Mac spike 2026-09-16 on BQAA: $172.17 / 2614 calls; sample branch $64.48. Prefer show --branch. Fleet CI + Codex proxy still DEFER. Unpriced: claude-fable-5-1.
entries.plainTitle: receipt: itemized coding-agent costs shown on PRs
entries.whatItIs: An open-source tool that itemizes what an AI coding agent cost for the work behind a PR. In our Mac trial on one repo, it reported $172.17 across 2614 calls.
entries.whyItMatters: Kept as a follow-up for the coding loop, preferring its per-branch view; fleet CI use and a proxy for another coding CLI are still deferred, and one of our models had no price in it.

entries.title: Blind second reviewer (Claude Forge adversarial loop)
entries.why: Blind dual-LGTM on our team is now Astra + Fable (independent kickoffs; implementer ≠ reviewer). Applied 2026-09-16.
entries.plainTitle: A blind second reviewer, from an adversarial review loop
entries.whatItIs: An open-source project whose adversarial review loop uses a blind second reviewer.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook: our two blind reviews now come from two separate reviewer seats, each started independently, and the implementer is not one of the reviewers.

entries.title: Multi-agent coordination patterns (Anthropic)
entries.why: Names orchestrator/router failure modes — especially silent misroute. Action for us: ambiguous route → ask Haiyuan, never silent SendToAgent.
entries.plainTitle: Multi-agent coordination patterns: avoid silent misroutes
entries.whatItIs: A model maker’s blog post that names the ways orchestrator and router agents fail, above all the silent misroute, where work is quietly sent to the wrong place.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook: when a route is unclear, our bots ask Haiyuan instead of silently handing the work to another agent.

entries.title: Chief-of-staff intake + visible group rooms
entries.why: Route default asks through Agent Manage Bot; use Field Brief and Coding EM rooms when the handoff itself must be visible. Written handoff contracts (goal, owner, artifact path, return shape) cut silent dropoffs between Manage and specialists.
entries.plainTitle: Chief-of-staff intake and visible group rooms for handoffs
entries.whatItIs: Requests go through the manager bot by default, and the Field Brief and coding-loop group rooms are used when the handoff itself must be visible. Handoffs are written with a goal, owner, artifact path and return shape.
entries.whyItMatters: In playbook: written handoff contracts cut silent drop-offs between the manager bot and the specialist bots.

entries.title: Routine fire proxy on the usage dashboard

entries.title: Uncle Bob agent code-quality loop — short instructions, small steps, automated gates, then mutation and CRAP hardening and Gherkin acceptance
entries.why: Code-quality loop for coding agents in five stages, as summarized from an image Haiyuan shared on 2026-10-10: short instructions, small steps, automated gates, hardening with mutation testing and CRAP scores, and acceptance written in Gherkin (Given / When / Then). No URL: that image is the only source and its author is not identified, so href is this Lab page, not a source, and the Uncle Bob name is how the loop was shared, not checked here. CRAP (change risk) is comp² × (1 − cov)³ + comp per function, where comp is its cyclomatic complexity and cov its test coverage from 0 to 1; over 30 is the usual cut-off, and a function whose complexity is over 30 scores over 30 at any coverage, so it needs splitting, not more tests. Already applied, per the harness playbook: dual review → human merge. Also applied: #522, report-only mutmut on the BQAA SDK, schedule or manual only and never a merge gate: 972 mutants, 70.9% score, 272 survivors (kick-ledger numbers; (972 − 272) / 972 would be 72.0%, so check #522's report before quoting a killed count), the survivors now a nightly-audit follow-up. Not yet: CRAP scoring and Gherkin acceptance. Design notes drafted 2026-10-11 (nothing run): report-only CRAP next to #522 (coverage.py plus radon or lizard, schedule or manual, never a gate, its top functions fed to the nightly audit as test-writing themes), and Coding EM kick done-when written as Given / When / Then, each Then a check code can run, or tagged for review when it needs judgment. Fit: code decides done, the closed proof loop, disproof review (reviewers take their rejection criteria from the done-when), and the mutation-testing Lab cards (Kanon's a guard must be able to fail, corralai's planted faults). Caveats: CRAP rewards coverage, not assertions, so a test that runs a line without checking it lowers CRAP while that line's mutants survive, so CRAP sits next to mutation, not in place of it; per-function coverage from line spans is approximate, and radon and lizard count complexity differently, so one tool is picked and pinned; Gherkin here covers the kick contract, not executable acceptance tests inside the SDK, which would need step definitions and a runner. Any workflow, kick-template or playbook change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: ScaleMAS: bounded sharing during collection
entries.why: ScaleMAS (Qi et al.) has identical, role-free agents work asynchronously through one append-only store per task: they publish results with references to what they built on, search it with BM25 plus a decaying citation weight (at most 8 messages per call), and visit messages by address. With a 9B model the authors report BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rising from 38.1% with one agent to 65.3% with 16; on SWE-bench Verified, 4 agents matching the 80.0% of 8 independent agents with about half the tokens (15.3M against 28.3M per example); and, at 8 agents, BrowseComp-Plus falling from 60.0% to 40.8% when the citation weight is removed. Proposed experiment (playbook §6, Field Brief pipeline): with the three existing collector seats and equal total token budgets, compare the current pack workflow (one pack per seat, all read for the brief) against task-local sharing of intermediate results with bounded BM25 retrieval, then add citation weighting as a separate ablation. Measure verified coverage and false claims in the selected final brief, duplicate tool calls, total tokens and elapsed time; the runs include a misleading but popular finding and a collector dropout. Adopt only if verified output improves or equal quality costs less; stop if citation ranking amplifies false findings. Promotion only via §16's existing gate (three clean runs, rollback tested, receipt complete); reviewer findings stay out of the shared pool so review stays blind. Caveats: the three third-party benchmarks run on 100 items each (the first 100, or all of FATE-H) with no variance or error bars reported for the headline numbers, and are scored Pass@N: the group counts as right if any of its N agents is right (so part of the 1-to-16 rise is extra tries), and choosing the final answer is called orthogonal and never tested, which is why the experiment scores the selected brief. ScaleMAS's large relative gains over debate and shared-context baselines are on Contradiction Audit, the authors' own LLM-built benchmark, where a contradiction counts as found if any reported pair includes its edited snippet and false reports cost nothing: debate and shared-context baselines never exceed 7% there in the 9B runs, while ScaleMAS reaches 29.4% at 16 agents and 50.9% at 128. Citation-quality evidence is partly circular: among examples whose correct answer cites a message, 85% of the most-cited fifth of messages lie on a correct answer's evidence chain against 29% of the least-cited, but that chain is traced through citations, as the authors acknowledge; messages naming gold evidence do draw about twice the citations of those naming other sources. Self-citations and replies that correct or contradict a message also add to its weight, so popularity cannot stand in for verification. The cap bounds each call, not total context or cost: an agent's intake grows with how often it reads, and on FATE-M at 8 agents BM25-only ranking read twice the tokens of the default (5.7M against 2.7M) under the same cap. The store is discarded after each task, so it is no evidence against our durable memory loop. The paper's role-free agents run with no human gate or reviewer, so the results do not justify replacing our lanes, human gates or blind review. Nothing has been run; any workflow change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Deeper, not bigger: a depth check for briefs
entries.why: Felix Rieseberg's post "How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models" (2026-10-13) names four types of ambition: speed (the same work in less time), altitude (going up in abstraction to the outcome rather than the individual task), depth (considering a task the way a field-leading expert would, going one level deeper to the underlying data, tools and problems) and range (drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface). For depth it gives a prompt asking for "a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one": before rewriting the prompt, the model says what a top professional in the field would do that was not asked for, names the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested, names the specific methods and tools they would use, and says what, other than the model or the user, would show the result is right. Adopted: an optional depth-check step in research and draft briefs (vault templates/research-draft-brief.md; Decision Maps/Decisions/2026-10-15-depth-check-brief-step.md) with four prompts: what a top professional would do that the brief does not ask for; the rawest sources rather than summaries; that professional's specific methods and tools; and what outside check shows the result is right, which points to our existing blind review and done receipts rather than adding a new check. Already had: an outside judge (the post: do not ask the model to judge itself) in blind Astra/Fable review instead of self-grading, and in our code-decides-done checks where a tool can verify; outcome-level goals (the post's altitude) in routines such as the PR board sweep and the stuck-job check (the Coding EM kick pickup check); and specialist bot lanes, though they are only a partial match for the post's range, which means bringing several fields into one task. Nothing has been measured yet, and the post reports no results for the prompt either, only that it often helps the author. Not in the playbook: the step lives in the vault template and the Decision note. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: lastlight-pr-gate: push gate needing a fresh-session review at the exact SHA
entries.why: Pre-tool-use hook plugin for a coding-agent CLI whose rule is that no unreviewed commit reaches a remote: a push needs a review recorded locally at that exact SHA, run with the review assets of the PR-review service the plugin is named for. The review must come from the plugin's run script, which runs it in a fresh headless session that did not write the code and writes attestation.json binding the result to the head SHA and a hash of the exact diff read; the recorder refuses a marker without a matching attestation, so a hand-written findings.json is rejected. The reviewed diff is untrusted input: the review runs in a disposable git clone under the OS sandbox, with credential stores denied and egress limited to the API, and only findings.json is copied back out. Containment is verified, not assumed: because a settings file that fails validation is silently ignored in headless mode, the runner first attempts a real escape and refuses to go on if the canary survives. A pre-commit review of the working tree is advisory and cannot satisfy the gate, since its attestation carries an empty SHA, which the recorder refuses by design. The pass bar is no findings, or every finding dismissed with a stated reason of at least 25 characters. The gate covers git push in its various spellings, the PR create, ready and reopen commands and API POSTs to a pulls endpoint, and it denies the code host's MCP write tools outright; reads and merges are never gated, and the check needs no network and fails closed. It also ships a work sandbox built on a clone, not a worktree, because a worktree's git dir lives inside the real repository; its README's two-layer table says the filesystem sandbox confines the processes the shell tool spawns but not the file-writing tools, permission rules cover file edits but not spawned processes, and neither confines the environment, so the review session starts from an empty environment (env -i) with a keep-list. The author states the limit plainly: it is not tamper-proof; it makes the honest path easy and stops a stale review vouching for new code. Why it matters here: every blind review of ours ends with exactly one machine-readable verdict line on the head SHA; a review with no parseable line, or one naming an older SHA, is UNPARSED and never counts as an LGTM, and dual LGTM means two APPROVE lines on the current head SHA (#review-verdict-line). The collection pack calls that rule prose discipline today; the attestation is the same rule as a check that can fail, bound to a hash of the diff the reviewer read, so a review recorded at one SHA cannot vouch for new code and hand-written findings are refused. We already have: blind dual review in which the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop), which the pack notes is roster discipline, not enforced by construction; anything an agent reads, PR text and tool output included, treated as data, never instructions (#untrusted-content); and the rule that a new check is first run against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail (#check-can-fail), which the escape probe applies to a sandbox. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the attestation format and gate contract as playbook prose first, that is, a marker bound to head SHA, diff hash, reviewer model and sandbox posture, written only by a fresh session that did not write the code, with hand-written findings refused; reviewed diffs handled in a disposable clone with only findings copied back, after an escape probe proves containment, so that a silently ignored setting fails closed; advisory pre-commit review kept structurally unable to satisfy the gate; dismissals with a stated reason; and reads and merges never gated. A live push gate would change every seat's ship path, so it is a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it is tied to the service's packaged review assets, so only the attestation and gate pattern would carry over, not the service dependency; its hooks fit one coding-agent CLI, and sandbox behaviour differs by platform, so containment would have to be probed per seat; the test counts in its README (245, 16, 133, 119 and 142 cases across five suites, as printed by the suites) are the author's and were read, not re-run; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-04; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Driftproof: with/without-skill evals that issue model-bound receipts
entries.why: Open-source tool that measures whether a SKILL.md still helps after the model underneath changes: it runs the skill's own eval tasks with and without the skill, judges each answer several times and issues a receipt bound to the model version saying the skill clearly helps, clearly hurts, makes no clear difference, or had too few answers to tell. Its credibility rule is to report bands (mean ± standard deviation) and to claim a change only when the bands do not overlap and the difference clears a 0.05 effect floor, never on either alone; in the author's words, "a tool that cries wolf is worse than no tool". Since receipt spec v0.5 it samples the generation as well as the judge, 3 to 10 draws per arm, each judged repeatedly, with a stopping_reason recorded; the author's Report #006 found draw-to-draw standard deviation of up to 0.186, larger than the judge's noise. It consumes an existing eval format for skills, and a run refuses up front if the projected calls or dollars exceed its caps (DEV_MAX_CALLS, DEV_MAX_USD). Reference data from the author's Report #005 (30 cells): a skill's cost when it fires is driven mainly by the input it makes the model pull in rather than by its own length (input delta against cost r = +0.92, the skill's own length r = +0.33), and one 738-token skill drew 34 times its own size in extra input. Why it matters here: the collection pack notes that our skills are mirrored across six seats on one-time verdicts that nobody re-checks when the model underneath changes, while verdicts age because the substrate moves. A dated receipt bound to the model version answers the recalibrate-or-retire question (does each rule still earn its place when a model changes?) with evidence instead of memory, and the pack places it next to Harness Wrangler's card (paired harness experiments, ablation, trigger sets) on an axis Wrangler does not price: model-bound skill receipts over time and the marginal cost of firing. We already have: before a skill or prompt change is promoted, a few saved runs are replayed to confirm nothing regressed, and a replay pass means nothing broke, not that the change is good (#replay-check); three runs can catch a large regression, but three clean runs do not show that a smaller one is absent (#detection-floor); and long runs inherit $0 spend without Haiyuan's approval (#run-limits). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved), as promotion-gate prose with one pilot skill named: each shared skill carries 3 to 5 human-approved eval cases grounded in claims its SKILL.md makes; a with/without run issues a dated receipt naming the model version; the decision rule is band non-overlap plus the 0.05 floor, with generation sampled, so a single judged answer never decides; runs refuse before spending past call and dollar caps, and the same receipt prices the marginal cost of firing (the input pulled in, not the skill's length); and a model change in any seat re-queues receipts for the skills that seat loads. Caveats: this card is the pattern plus the author's reference data; any metered run is spend and needs Haiyuan, who also chooses between a subscription and a metered API path, and standing scheduled runs would be recurring spend; judge noise is real, and bands reduce it without removing it, so the author advises re-running a surprising verdict before acting on it; eval cases need approval skill by skill; every report number is the author's run, not ours; Apache-2.0, 2 stars, created 2026-07-28; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: keel: verifiers try to refute serious findings; review depth is priced
entries.why: Workflow plugin for a coding-agent CLI that plans, builds and independently verifies a change, with the verification depth priced per change, verification only: gates only about $0.2, Basic about $0.25 to 0.5, Standard about $1.4 to 4.3 and Maximum about $2.7 to 7.6. Its doctrine is that a false alarm is a cost, not a bonus: serious findings go to separate verifiers that try to refute them, a finding QA "proved" that keel cannot reproduce becomes "unclear", and anything not checked is labelled "not verified". The author's measurements (a blind-scored set of 8 changes with 17 known defects, keel 1.0, October 2026): one plain reviewer, about $0.22, found 15.5 with 4 false alarms in 8 runs; Basic, about $0.34, found 15.3 with 0 false alarms in 24 runs; Standard, about $2.4, found 16.3; Maximum, about $5, found 17 with 0 false alarms in 8 runs. Counting only must- and should-fix items, Basic and Standard each found 15 of 17 and Maximum 14. The author says plainly that keel does not make review cheaper, it makes it cleaner, and that on this set Basic's fix list matched Standard's on every change. Hard steps (confirmations, the verification record before a finish, and keel's own git step: no secret files, no AI attribution, no commit on main) are hooks and scripts, not prompts; every end of work shows tokens, dollars and plan share per agent; and tasks (a branch and folder each) and sessions (a handoff note) are separate lanes that never mix in one conversation. Why it matters here: the collection pack calls it the first priced false-alarm measurement for our disproof-review lane, and notes that our reviews state rejection criteria up front but never cost a false alarm or report not verified as a first-class label inside the fix list, nor count a false alarm's cost inside our one-fix-round budget (now three fix rounds, then escalate: Haiyuan 2026-10-20 02:39 PT). We already have: blind reviewers who ask what would make a change unacceptable, name 2–3 rejection criteria from the task contract before reading the diff, return evidence on FAIL and list what was tried on PASS (#disproof-review); final done reports with a NOT VERIFIED section, what was not checked, never omitted (#done-receipt); public PR review comments from our review seats that carry only P0s, P1s and merge-blocking P2s (#review-posts-blockers); and the always-on play of skills for advisory policy and hooks for must-hold rules (#em-loop), which keel follows for its hard steps. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved), as review-contract prose with no install: a refutation pass by a separate verifier before findings become must- or should-fix, with unreproduced "proofs" downgraded to unclear and unchecked areas labelled not verified finding by finding; depth chosen by price, with the price shown before and after (gates only, basic, deep), defaulting to shallow unless the change touches money, access, migrations or widely depended-on code; per-agent token and dollar rows in end-of-work reports; and hard steps (the verification record before finish, git hygiene) kept in hooks and scripts, not prompts. Caveats: the numbers are the author's single test set (8 changes, 17 defects; Maximum one run per change), directionally useful but not our fleet's rates; it runs in one coding-agent CLI only today; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-15; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: rollcage-guard: one secret-guard rules file for four coding-agent tools
entries.why: Single local binary (a signed, notarized build that runs locally and sends nothing) that installs one rules file as a pre-tool-use guard in four coding-agent tools, through each tool's own hook. It blocks reads of secret files (.env files, ~/.ssh, a cloud provider's credentials folder, *.pem and *.key files, infrastructure state files, service-account JSON; .env.example is allowed), environment dumps (printenv, /proc/*/environ, keychain reads), inline interpreter one-liners that read environment variables, and destructive commands; it asks before risky, cloud and production commands and before pushes to protected branches; before a git commit or git push it scans the staged changes and outgoing commits for keys; and it blocks exfiltration domains. Where a tool's hook cannot ask, ask becomes a block. explain "COMMAND" previews a verdict, and status and log show coverage and recent blocks, with keys masked in the log. The README states its limits: it fails open on an internal error, it is a guardrail, not a sandbox, it matches patterns, and it covers only agents that have hooks. The same rules are also offered as an advisory public MCP server, which advises while the hook enforces. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our kept guards are single-seat (cheat-drill probes one coding-agent CLI's hooks; tamperproof and bouncer are shaped for that CLI) while the fleet runs six seats, and this is one deterministic rules file for several CLIs, with a key scan at commit and push, the moment a key actually leaves, and an explain preview so a rule can be tested before it fires. We already have: a forbidden.md ban on secret disclosure, which the pack notes is enforced only as per-seat prose, and the always-on play that keeps skills for advisory policy and hooks for must-hold rules, no secrets in the diff among them (#em-loop). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a reversible trial of one shared rules file on the two of our seats whose CLIs it supports, warn and log first, then block, with uninstall as the rollback; the staged and outgoing-commit key scan at commit and push; an explain-style preview and a masked block log, plus a cheat-drill pass before trusting any coverage number; and the guard kept local-only, without the public MCP endpoint. Fleet-wide standing enforcement would change shared seat config, a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it fails open by design, so a guard bug allows the call and the log has to be watched; it matches patterns and is not a sandbox; a third tool it supports may match the hook surface of one more of our seats, but that fit was not verified, so no coverage of that seat is claimed; the advisory MCP endpoint was not fetched or graded; it is the open-source core of a commercial desktop app, and only the core would be tried; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-14; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: pair-mailbox: one writer, sealed-patch critic, turns end on a mailbox read
entries.why: Two-agent pair protocol for independent coding-agent CLIs (Python 3 standard library only; tmux and git required; profiles for six CLIs). Exactly one agent holds write authority, and its MCP server enforces the single-writer rule at the protocol level, logging refusals to an append-only audit transcript; the critic works read-only and proposes changes only as SHA-256-sealed patch files (mode 0600) whose hash the writer verifies immediately before applying them, a hash seal, not a signature, as the author says. Its core delivery rule is "The Mailbox Is the Guarantee, Delivery Is the Accelerator": a turn ends with a bounded pair_read(wait_seconds=N), so an agent is never idle with unread mail, while pair_deliver, which types a pointer into the peer's tmux pane, is best-effort only, since a full-screen TUI hides it. Mailbox files are atomic and numbered monotonically under flock, and the peer or a watchdog confirms allowlisted [y/N] prompts. An autonomy setting decides how far the pair runs alone: the default, auto, works a round through to a finished PR with no human word; semi needs recorded evidence and one human ok at verify; secrets, deploys, migrations, deletions and git history stop the pair at every level. Its own table names a weakness: pair_evidence is agent-reported and the close gate trusts it, so rounds refuse to close without it, but it is self-declared. Why it matters here: it is the enforced version of our written-handoff discipline for two live seats. A server-refused single writer plus sealed-patch review is implementer ≠ reviewer with a code boundary, and ending each turn with a bounded read makes the mailbox a guarantee rather than a hope, preventing the stall where an agent sits idle with unread mail in headless tmux work. We already have: every handoff from Manage to a specialist carries a machine-readable packet (#handoff-packet), and the pack notes that Manage handoffs already assume this discipline in prose; the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop); done means a concrete, deterministic check passed, such as tests green, the expected file present, a commit pushed or a live URL at HTTP 200, and self-reports are advisory only (#code-decides-done); merges, payments, unsolicited publishes and agent deletion require Haiyuan (#thesis); and agent-perch's card has the file-mailbox-over-keystrokes rule, to which pair-mailbox adds the bounded read that ends each turn. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved), in semi only: for a two-seat build and review pair, exactly one writer enforced by the coordination layer with refusals audit-logged, and a read-only critic proposing hash-sealed patches verified immediately before apply; turns that end with a bounded mailbox read, pane typing being only an accelerator; a close that needs recorded evidence plus one human ok, with secrets, deploys, migrations, deletions and history as hard stops at every level; and self-declared evidence replaced by our code-decides-done checks (tests, file, commit, live URL) before any close counts. The default, auto, reaches a finished PR with no human word, which the collection pack rules out under Haiyuan's human gate; only semi with our existing merge gate fits. Caveats: pair_evidence is trusted self-report upstream and would have to be swapped as above; how far the server enforces the single-writer rule beyond the README and protocol summary was not code-audited; the installer edits several CLIs' configs, so any trial must be scoped and reversible; split sessions need bash 4 or newer; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-02; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat pilot, install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: whystuck: names why a quiet command stalled and prints the non-interactive fix
entries.why: One-file Python idle watchdog (zero dependencies, Python 3.9+): you run any command under it, and when the output goes quiet (--idle 20 by default) it inspects the live process tree and classifies the stall as a pager, an editor, a y/N prompt, a password prompt, watch mode, a lock, a stalled TCP connect (SYN_SENT only), a server, or busy (at least 25% of a core over 0.5 s), then prints the evidence and the non-interactive fix. --json gives a machine-readable result, --kill sends SIGTERM to the process group and then SIGKILL (with a subreaper on Linux), and --explain PID diagnoses a process that is already hung. The author reports 136 tests, including a mutation-style check that removing any rule must break a case, 9 real-process snapshots and real PTY runs per rule; --demo runs 8 scenarios offline. The README states its limits plainly: DNS stalls and established-but-silent connections are not diagnosed; the server class cannot tell a healthy server from an internally hung one; macOS is best-effort (ps and lsof only, with no syscall or lock-holder detail, while Linux gets the full /proc view) and was not tested on real macOS in v0.1; Windows is unsupported (it exits 2); and --json carries the last 4,000 characters of output, with a printed secrets warning. The author's prior-art search (8 query variants, 18 Oct 2026) found no standalone agent-agnostic live-stall diagnoser; the closest were per-agent prevention lists and kill-only timeout. Why it matters here: the collection pack notes that our launch watchdog knows that a seat went quiet, not why, and that the why is usually a pager, editor or prompt a headless seat will never answer. whystuck supplies the missing diagnosis layer, the cause and a non-interactive fix at the stall, plus --explain for after-the-fact triage of a wedged pane, and the pack places it beside kept agent-chain-doctor (silent-stop checks at startup) and Cliffhanger (conversational early stops), at the process layer neither covers. We already have: every long Mac run launched in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) that resumes the same session (#launch), next to the EM's 15-minute heartbeat, which does not replace the watchdog (#em-loop); Mac launch skills that document symptom → action failure branches, a ~540 s stall among them, and named long-run failure modes (crash, hang, stall, api-error) whose rule is to leave a machine-readable heartbeat saying whether the run finished and what killed it (#exception-first); the rule that a stale run resumes only after the old agent process is confirmed gone, else it is parked as an unknown outcome, checked by hand because the live watchdog still kills and resumes without that check (#watchdog-resume-safety); and the rule that a new check is first run against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail (#check-can-fail), which whystuck's remove-a-rule test applies to its stall rules. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the stall taxonomy as watchdog vocabulary (pager, editor, y/N prompt, password prompt, watch mode, lock, stalled connect, server, busy), each paired with its non-interactive fix, so a stale-pane alert names the cause and the remedy, not just the elapsed silence; a trial of whystuck --explain on one seat against the next genuinely wedged pane, read-only diagnosis first, with removing the binary as the rollback and --kill only after the diagnosis is trusted; and the remove-a-rule-must-break-a-test check on any stall rule we ship. Wiring it into the live watchdog would be a separate Haiyuan decision: the watchdog's no-auto-resume redesign is parked and reopens only on Haiyuan's ask (#watchdog-resume-safety), and the playbook says not to fleet-replace the watchdog without that ask (#exception-first). Caveats: the author has not tested the macOS path and our seats run on a Mac, so the trial is itself the platform test; DNS stalls and established-but-silent connections stay undiagnosed; after a --kill, a resume would still wait until the old agent process is confirmed gone (#watchdog-resume-safety); the --json output tail can carry secrets if the command prints them, and secrets stay out of vault notes and hub commits (#checklist); the test counts are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-18; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: watchdog-kit: change-only alerts for scheduled jobs that escalate once if ignored
entries.why: Change-only monitoring primitives for one Mac's scheduled jobs (Python 3.9+, zero dependencies, no daemon; you schedule it with launchd or cron and read the exit code). A state machine per job id fires on NEW, CHANGED and RECOVER, stays silent on PERSIST, and fires ESCALATE once after --escalate-after (7 days by default), so a long-ignored problem cannot fade out by being consistently ignored. Exit codes are the interface: 0 when nothing changed (including a job still broken and already known), 1 for NEW, CHANGED or ESCALATED, 2 for recoveries only, and 3 for a scan error, deliberately never folded into 0 ("a monitor that cannot read anything must not look like one that read everything and found it fine"). Three false-positive traps are designed out, each with a named test: a poll gap is not liveness (liveness is a run-counter delta and staleness is period × slack, never polling cadence); a non-zero exit is static history (reading launchd's last exit code twice is not "failed again", and a strike advances only on changed evidence); and a first observation is a BASELINE, never an alert. The period is inferred from the job's plist (StartInterval or StartCalendarInterval) rather than copied into config, and a 0-byte log is its own state (QUIET). A runs plugin audits recorded agent completions without a model: COMPLETED_EMPTY (done with a null or empty result), COMPLETED_THIN (done with tokens under the spec's min_tokens) and RUNNING_STUCK; it opens the database mode=ro, allowlists SQL identifiers to [A-Za-z0-9_], and deliberately avoids immutable=1, which would skip the WAL and read stale data. The author observed it on a real machine with 91 LaunchAgents: round 1 reported NEW 18 (exit 1), round 2 suppressed PERSIST 18, and round 3 reported RECOVER 1 and PERSIST 53. It observes and classifies only; remediation is out of scope. Why it matters here: the collection pack calls it the alert-fatigue half of our miss-watch that we never wrote down. Our Collection :44 detector and the usage dashboard's routine fire proxy report state; this adds transition semantics (speak on NEW, CHANGED or RECOVER, stay silent on PERSIST, escalate once so silence cannot become permanent) plus two liveness rules that, per the pack, our launchd jobs need verbatim: liveness as a run-counter delta, and a last exit code as history. The pack also reads the runs audit as kept overclaim's lesson put into practice (deterministic external signals contradicting a completed claim, read-only and WAL-aware), and exit 3, never 0, as our gap-not-zero rule written as an interface contract. We already have: Collection's :44 miss-watch as the sole Field Brief detector when the :34 brief never wakes (#field-brief-12h); the routine fire proxy on the usage dashboard, coarse cron fires per week labeled PROXY (#usage); a receipt line for every routine run, written even when nothing happened, while chat stays quiet on success (#receipt-line); open decision-queue items re-raised to Haiyuan once after 3+ days, never daily (#decision-queue), the same escalate-once shape; a usage collector that prints STALE_SOURCES: and exits non-zero instead of publishing a silently old date (#usage-freshness), and a 2026-10-08 false stale alarm read from agent-dir mtimes despite same-day receipts, fixed on 2026-10-11 (#usage-false-stale); a failed lookup reported as an access gap, never as zero or quiet (#negative-claim-check), and a check that examined nothing reported as a gap, never a pass (#check-can-fail); and the rule that a completion claim counts only when the session record backs it (#claim-vs-record). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the NEW / CHANGED / RECOVER / PERSIST / ESCALATE-once state machine for Mac scheduled-job monitoring, with exit codes as the contract and a scan error as 3, never 0; liveness by run-counter delta with period × slack staleness, the period inferred from the plist, and silence on the first-round baseline; and a trial of the runs audit shape (done but empty, done but thin, running stuck) over recorded agent runs, read-only and WAL-aware, with thresholds from our own distributions. The pack frames the trial as one machine's launchd jobs, observe and classify only, with no remediation. Caveats: v0.1.0; the author states that the launchd period inference is biased late; min_tokens must be calibrated per workload or it is noise; it is single-machine by design, and the author says fleet alerting stays with Alertmanager-class tools; the 91-agent rounds are the author's run, not ours; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-18; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: plan-validation: rehearses a plan's scope in a disposable worktree before coding
entries.why: Plan-rehearsal skills, shipped as a plugin for one coding-agent CLI and as skills for another, built on one idea: rehearse the plan before coding. validation-args is read-only: it finds the correct plan and spec copies and prepares the invocation. validate-plan reviews and revises the plan, rehearses the selected scope in a disposable worktree against a recorded Git base with approved focused checks, gets an independent review and renders an HTML evidence report. revise-prompt critiques and scores a prompt and never executes it. Coverage is checked in both directions (each requirement has a task and a test; each task serves an approved requirement), scope changes are made visible (phases, tasks and dependencies before and after a revision), and the original and revised docs, fingerprints, actual results and review findings are kept as a cross-session handoff under ~/.local/share/plan-validation/. Planning docs stay uncommitted, and the handoff grants no merge or deploy authority. The README is plain about its boundaries: it is a pilot release; the example is an authored fixture, not a benchmark; the renderer checks structure, arithmetic and fingerprints but cannot prove a review happened or a test result is true; scores are judgments, not probabilities; a worktree isolates files, not network or database side effects; and rehearsal can duplicate substantial implementation work. An agent-free demo (scripts/demo.py, standard library only, no model calls) renders a labeled Not-ready example. Why it matters here: the collection pack notes that our EM loop reviews plans by reading them, so nothing executes a plan's own instructions before a seat commits hours to them, and a plan pointing at a nonexistent file or a failing command is found by the implementer hours in. This is the rehearsal step: a disposable-worktree exercise against a recorded base, coverage checked both ways (the pack notes that the orphan-task direction is the one our reviews miss), and a fingerprint-bound evidence report that survives the session boundary, with the authority boundary stated correctly (a handoff is not permission). The pack also reads the admission that the renderer cannot prove a review happened as the evidence honesty our receipts require. We already have: the artifact chain intent.md → spec.md → plan.md → PR + tests → dual review → human merge, in which plan.md holds the ordered slices, files to touch, test plan and done definition, the implementer works from it and reviewers check the PR against it (#em-loop); blind reviewers who name 2–3 rejection criteria from the intent/spec/plan done-when before reading the diff (#disproof-review); for multi-file doc or policy folds, a check of every claim against the newest live sources and a dry-run rebase before blind review (#review-round-breaker); for bug jobs, a repro artifact linked before the implementer launches, with the implementer's first commit being that failing test (#coding-em-kicks); handoffs that pass ownership, not transcripts, through a machine-readable packet (#handoff-packet); done receipts that summarize what the harness can prove happened, not what the model claims (#done-receipt); merge by Haiyuan only (#coding); and one SDK repo that forbids checking in intent.md, plan.md or spec.md, so those stay in the vault or local-only (#em-loop). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): EM plans above a size threshold get a rehearsal step that exercises the plan's selected scope in a disposable worktree against a recorded Git base with approved focused checks before implementation starts; coverage is checked both ways (requirement → task and test, task → approved requirement), and the scope diff (phases, tasks, dependencies) is shown whenever a plan is revised; the original and revised docs, fingerprints, actual results and findings are kept as the cross-session handoff, uncommitted and granting no merge or deploy authority; and every rehearsal command is inspected before it runs, because a worktree is not a sandbox for network or database effects, and long runs already inherit 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval (#run-limits). The pack suggests a plugin trial on one seat, with the rehearsal cost budgeted per plan rather than made universal. Caveats: a pilot release whose example is an authored fixture, not a benchmark, and nothing has been measured here; the renderer cannot prove a review happened; rehearsal can duplicate substantial implementation work; it ships for two coding-agent CLIs; Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-10-14; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: downshift: deterministic per-subagent model routing with a built-in control arm
entries.why: Single Go binary (beta) for deterministic subagent model routing, with no model in the loop, prompt-free and fail-open: a pre-tool-use hook classifies each delegated task and rewrites only that subagent's model and effort, choosing from the session's own small, mid and frontier list. It is conservative under doubt: rules R1–R9 carry invariant tests, unconfident upshifts and frontier picks are held, a guessed baseline downshifts only to small, and risky wording clears confidence; a project tier floor in .downshift/policy.json raises and never lowers; secrets, payments, auth and destructive work keep a floor; and a quota gate holds a rewrite to a model with no credit, with stale snapshots no longer holding after 1 h. Every decision is visible (a stderr line per spawn, session --tree, and doctor with a fix per failure), and per-child tokens, catalog-priced cost and end status are recorded. Its stance is measure instead of believe: a built-in control group leaves about 1 in 10 spawns unrouted, and stats and report compare routed against control cost per completed task with a confidence interval, along an evidence ladder of dated rungs (Rung D reached once on 2026-10-15; Rung E not measured). The author's measured A/B (2026-10-15, one operator, one coding-agent CLI, hidden tests): on mechanical one-per-subagent pieces, the ceiling case, cost fell 12% at the same 12/12 accepted; on natural tasks most spawns were held and the difference is not attributable to routing. The rewrite was observed honored on that CLI (2026-10-06), is inferred on a second and unconfirmed on a third, and usage capture works on the first only. Why it matters here: the collection pack sets it apart from the kept per-message effort card: this is deterministic per-subagent model choice with a permanent control arm, which the pack calls the first routing proposal to ship its own falsification rig (1 in 10 unrouted, judged by cost per completed task rather than tokens saved). The pack notes that our max-effort defaults spend frontier prices on delegated mechanics and that every earlier routing proposal, the kept effort card included, lacks a control arm, so savings claims are unfalsifiable. For a fleet whose standing rule is max-effort defaults, the pack names the adoptable parts as the guardrails (doubt holds, floors only raise, fail-open) and the control-group accounting, even if routing itself stays shadow, and it reads the honest not-attributable result on natural tasks as the negative-result reporting our cards demand. We already have: a shadow posture for decision-layer gates, which log and never block (#worth-running-scope), and a gate dominated by one verdict must beat the constant "always the majority verdict" on hand-checked minority calls before it goes active, or it stays shadow (#constant-baseline); promotion notes that say three runs only catch large regressions and list every case that got worse (#detection-floor); a replay check whose pass means nothing broke, not that the change is good (#replay-check); long runs that inherit $0 spend without Haiyuan's approval (#run-limits); and per-CLI quota and health cards on the usage dashboard (#usage). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the measurement discipline, not (yet) the routing. Any future model or effort routing in our fleet ships with a permanent unrouted control share and reports cost per completed task (with rework), routed against control, never tokens saved alone; routing guardrails, if ever enabled, follow downshift's shape (doubt holds, floors only raise, fail-open, risky categories keep a floor, and a quota gate with stale-snapshot expiry); and downshift is trialed in observe or shadow posture only, on one seat whose CLI it supports, to check its per-child cost and end-status accounting against our usage dashboard. Live routing would conflict with the max-effort defaults, so it is a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: beta; the rewrite is observed honored on one CLI only (inferred on a second, unconfirmed on a third), and usage capture works on that CLI only; per the pack, the author has not yet unlocked a strict cost-per-completed-task definition either; the A/B is one operator's run on 2026-10-15, the author's and not ours; Apache-2.0, 6 stars, 4 issues, created 2026-09-20; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: landscape: read-only preflight that checks coverage before any install or build
entries.why: Read-only capability preflight for the coding-agent harness that one of our seats runs, offered as a plugin for that harness, a portable agent skill and a CLI (find, analyze, brief, status): you describe one change in natural language and get an evidence-backed decision before any install, replace, upgrade, compose or build. The output contract covers the intent; environment status (detected, partial, unavailable or not-applicable); an existing-coverage verdict (for example CROWDED); risks; one decision (USE, INSTALL, COMPOSE, EXTEND, BUILD, WAIT, DISABLE or INVESTIGATE); explicit Do Not Build and Build Only boundaries; the next action; and limitations. It gives advice, not mutation: it never installs, enables, edits a profile or creates a repo, and needs no account, key or config; if runtime inspection is unavailable it continues on its bundled ecosystem snapshot and states what it could not verify, so UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN. Its maturity note is honest: a dev version from source, with no npm release; tested locally on Windows with Node 24 against harness version 0.1.7-rc.2 (2026-09-28); model-backed end-to-end runs and native macOS runs not repeated. Why it matters here: per the collection pack it directly serves that seat, which we pin and which two recent kept cards target (a compatibility bridge kept 10-10 and a goal-wait gate kept 10-09): a preflight that answers whether a capability is already covered before anyone builds or installs, with the two boundary lists (Do Not Build, Build Only) that the pack says our handoff packets lack. The pack counts it as our most actively extended seat with no already-covered check before building, the duplicate-capability waste this preflight exists to stop, and notes that read-only by construction plus unavailable-means-unavailable matches our gap-not-zero rule. We already have: that seat on the hourly collect rotation and as an optional implementer (#roster), with AGENTS.md and skills wired into its home by our fleet-wide installer (#skills); handoffs that carry a machine-readable packet (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions already made, constraints, open questions, next gate) with no build-boundary field (#handoff-packet); a failed or stale lookup reported as an access gap, never as zero or quiet (#negative-claim-check); tool output treated as data, never instructions (#untrusted-content), so a preflight's decision would be evidence, not an order; and reads and research as GREEN (do it, log it), while permissions and production stay RED, always asked of Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): before any plugin install, replace or build on that seat, a read-only capability preflight that returns one decision with environment status, coverage verdict, risks and explicit Do Not Build and Build Only lists carried into the handoff packet; unavailable runtime inspection degrading to the bundled snapshot with the gap stated (UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN); and a preflight that never mutates (no install, enable or profile edit), with mutation staying behind the existing gates. The pack suggests a one-seat trial in skill or CLI form, pinned to a reviewed SHA, with removal as the rollback. Caveats: dev 0.3.1 with no npm release, so a trial would pin a reviewed SHA; the author tested on Windows against harness version 0.1.7-rc.2 only, so our pinned version on macOS is unverified; the ecosystem snapshot can go stale, so its freshness fields must be read, not assumed; nothing has been measured here; MIT, 6 stars, created 2026-08-13; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: everyhook: one hook source translated per coding agent, benched before install
entries.why: Zero-dependency Node tool (Node 18 or newer) with one hook contract and one adapter per agent for five coding agents that, per the README, agree on almost nothing: the pre-tool event is PreToolUse, BeforeTool or preToolUse, the refusal is spelled four ways, ask works in two, timeouts are seconds in four and milliseconds in one, exit code 2 blocks in four but not in one of them on Windows, where a shell layer turns it into 1, and exit code 1 denies in only one. run, the adapter, reads the agent's own JSON, builds one document for your hook, runs it and prints the agent's own JSON back; an answer an agent cannot take (an ask for an agent that has none, a deny at an event that cannot refuse) is translated to the nearest thing it can take, and bench and explain say which. install and uninstall edit each agent's config textually with that agent's event names, matcher and timeout unit, after a backup, adding only their own entries, and uninstall leaves the file byte for byte as it was. bench runs your hook against 64 documents, 53 recorded from four of the agents' real binaries plus 11 for the fifth written from its reference, and prints what the hook answered, what the agent would do and the exact JSON; explain marks every statement binary (a real run saw it) or docs (the reference says so). The author's evidence: the four binaries run on Windows 11 on 2026-10-17, CI on Windows, macOS and Linux runners on every push, and a 180-case translation table (5 agents × 6 events × 6 answers) pinned by tests. The gap is stated throughout: the fifth agent's binary was never run (its CLI needs a login), so every statement about it is docs and its fixtures say documented, not recorded. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we run six Mac CLI seats (#roster) and mirror the same guards by hand on each (force-push blocks, env-file protection, tool logging), so a guard fixed on one seat and silently missing on another is our standing failure mode. everyhook supplies the missing portability layer: one hook source, translation per seat, and a bench meant to show that the same hook means the same thing on each seat before it is installed. The pack reads the byte-preserving uninstall and the binary-versus-docs tags as matching our reversibility and observed-versus-claimed rules, and places it beside kept rollcage-guard (one guard's rules) at a distribution layer no kept card covers. We already have: a fleet-wide installer that wires the vault's contract file and skills into the seats' homes (#skills); the always-on play of skills for advisory policy and hooks for must-hold rules, no secrets in the diff, no push to main and no weakening tests during a fix among them (#em-loop); a run-log lesson in which one plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5 to 6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); GREEN, YELLOW and RED tiers by reversibility, with park-and-ask for anything that cannot be undone in under a minute (#gyr-authority), and a promotion gate that needs a rollback actually tried once (#promotion-gate); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it (#claim-vs-record), and Lab cards that call a practice applied only where this playbook says so (#lab-card-claims); and the rule that a new check is first seen to fail on a deliberately broken input and that a pass says what it examined (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): fleet guards (force-push, env-file, tool log) written once against one contract and translated per seat instead of hand-mirrored copies; a bench-only trial of our existing guards against recorded documents for two of our seats' agents before any install, with the bench output (the answer, the agent's effect and the exact JSON) required in the change packet; binary-versus-docs basis tags on every hook-behavior claim in our playbook; and byte-preserving uninstall, checked byte for byte, as the rollback standard. Installing it on live seats would edit their config, so that is a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the fifth agent is entirely unverified (docs only); the real-binary evidence is Windows-first, CI covers macOS and Linux, and our Mac seats would be the trial; answers an agent cannot express are degraded to the nearest one, so the degradation has to be read guard by guard; the binary runs, the 64 bench documents and the 180-case table are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-17; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-role-contracts: offline preflight that rejects self-review and stale handoffs
entries.why: Deterministic, offline preflight (Node 22.5 or newer; no API key, runtime or account) over a declared role, permissions, work scope and handoff. Before anything executes it rejects, each with a specific diagnostic: a task requesting a write outside its declared authority; implementer and reviewer collapsing into one declared role (self-review); a reviewed task or action that changed afterward (stale subject binding: the G1 digest covers the full bundle, policy, roles and routes included, plus the full task and the declared action, and a review or approval must bind that current digest); a filesystem mapping drifting from the declared action (the G2 filesystem-write adapter takes exactly a path and a content SHA-256 and rejects unknown parameters); and stale lifecycle or handoff declarations. Every result states that a PASS is not execution authority: it means the declarations are internally consistent under the checks that ran, while runtime identity, actual permissions, side-effect enforcement, evidence verification and execution approval remain separate and are stated as false. The digest gives integrity, not authenticity or authorization, and artifact paths and URLs are not immutable evidence. The author marks it stable 1.0.0 (npm latest, verified 2026-10-16), keeping the 0.5.0 public imports, API shapes, twelve schema identities, fail-closed claims and G1 digests, with a compatibility corpus that requires every other machine-report field, schema byte, fixed digest and raw CLI output to stay equal; the schema engine is a closed Draft-07 subset in which unsupported keywords fail loudly. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our chief-of-staff rooms and EM loop enforce implementer ≠ reviewer and task scope by prompt and by human reading, the layer that drifts when a handoff goes stale or a task is re-pointed after review. This moves three checks before execution and into code: scope against authority, role separation, and review bound to a digest, so that changing the task after review means the approval no longer matches. The pack calls that last rule the mechanical form of our dual-LGTM intent, stated more crisply than in any kept card, and places the checker beside kept agent-delegate-class handoff patterns and plan-validation (plan rehearsal), at a declaration layer neither checks. We already have: an EM loop in which the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it and the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop); review verdicts pinned to the head SHA, where a line naming an older SHA is UNPARSED and dual LGTM means two APPROVE lines on the current head SHA (#review-verdict-line); an approval re-check right before a RED action runs, confirming that the action still matches the approved item and that current authority still permits it, as policy text only (#approval-recheck); a machine-readable handoff packet (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open questions, next gate) whose completeness check is shadow only and never blocks (#handoff-packet); and RED actions such as send or publish, spend, merge, permissions and production, which always go to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): EM and chief-of-staff handoff packets that carry a declared role, permissions, work scope and reviewer, checked offline before a seat starts, with a write outside scope and an implementer who is also the reviewer both rejected; review and approval bound to a digest of the full bundle, task and action, so any change after review invalidates the approval until it is re-reviewed; and every PASS labeled declarations-consistent only, with execution authority, identity, enforcement and evidence verification kept as separate gates. The pack frames the trial as one EM flow with an offline check only and no control change; making it a gate on live handoffs would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: production adoption is not claimed by the author; the filesystem adapter covers exactly one operation (write_file with a path and content SHA-256), so broader tool semantics would need our own adapters; digests give integrity, not authenticity; the compatibility corpus is the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-09-30; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: agent-role-contracts: catches self-review and stale handoffs before work runs

A pass means the declarations agree, not that work may run.

entries.title: pinwash: post-session diff check for weakened pins, hooks and required checks
entries.why: Local-first, deterministic checker (Python 3.11 or newer, standard library only at scan time; no model, no network) that asks one question of a Git diff: did this change make an agent more able to claim done by weakening pins, hooks, permissions, required checks or bypass instructions? It does not execute the subject and enforces nothing. A session starts with pinwash session start in a clean worktree before the agent begins, and pinwash session review runs once the agent and every process it started have stopped; it asks, and a trusted controller passes --stopped only after making sure of that itself, since pinwash neither stops processes nor verifies that they stopped. The review runs three comparisons against the pinned baseline and the saved judge identity and writes a JSON report outside the project; each finding says what changed, why it matters and what to review next, and no findings does not prove that verification runs or that the product works. Verdicts are exact: Pass when all three invocations are clean; Held when they are clean except for an EXEMPTION_ADDED, meaning the session wrote an exemption record that only human review releases; Block on any exit 1; and anything else (exit 2, a timeout, unparseable output) is not judged, never a pass. Exemptions are per finding fingerprint and live on the base side only, with six required keys, an expiry no more than 180 days after creation and never a rule glob, and the exemption channel never exempts its own findings. The author reports that both installed wheels passed 690 tests in local Docker Linux verification, with a public acceptance receipt and frozen acceptance fixtures A1–A11, and states the limits plainly: Windows and macOS are not yet validated (package acceptance is Docker Linux only, and byte-identical JSON across platforms is specified but not CI-verified), and there is no 1.0 stability claim. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our agents can edit the very hooks and checks that judge them, and pinwash checks whether an agent edited the checks: gutted a hook into a non-stub that can no longer block, dropped a required context, or committed an exemption that quietly drops a finding once merged. The pack reads base-side-only exemptions plus Held-means-human-release as the right governance shape for a fleet whose agents can edit their own harness files, and the tool as directly trial-shaped, a post-session diff review on one seat's worktree. We already have: a test-tamper scan in which the EM and each reviewer read a code change's diff for tests skipped, deleted or focused, gutted assertions or a test command changed so it always passes, a green run after such a change being SUSPECT, never PASS; it is a prose rule with no hook installed, and no tamper incident is traced in our records yet (#claim-vs-record); the same scan also looks for || true added after a check and for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repo's hooks, and a check that examined nothing is a gap under NOT VERIFIED, never a pass (#check-can-fail); blind reviewers who scan code diffs for test tampering while attempting disproof (#disproof-review); hooks for must-hold rules, no weakening tests during a fix among them (#em-loop); and the rule that killing a stale session does not prove the old agent stopped, so a resume waits until the old process is confirmed gone, checked by hand (#watchdog-resume-safety), the same assurance pinwash leaves to a trusted controller before --stopped. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): agent sessions on harness-bearing repos run against a pinned baseline, a snapshot at session start and then a post-session review asking only whether pins, hooks, permissions or required checks were weakened; exemptions kept on the base side only, per finding fingerprint with an expiry of at most 180 days, and any exemption a session adds holding the work for human release; and a checker failure (a timeout, unparseable output, exit 2) treated as not judged, never a pass, and surfaced as a gap, not a zero. The pack frames the trial as report-only on one worktree, with the JSON report kept outside the project; using its verdicts to hold or block live work would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: Alpha 0.1.1 (SPEC 29) with no 1.0 claim; macOS and Windows are unvalidated, so a trial on our Mac would itself be the platform test; unknown_coverage rows need a local policy or they turn into noise, since ignored local settings files and hook logs surface every session; the 690 tests and the acceptance receipt are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-28; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: fael: per-file continuity ledger in .git, surfaced when the file is next touched
entries.why: Continuity ledger for agent work (an npm package for three coding-agent CLIs and MCP) that files each note where the code is touched and returns it where the code is touched. A hand-off written with fael add note, naming files (--files) and a key (--key), reaches the next session when it opens that file or its prompt names the key; an assignment, to a person by git user.name or to an agent, lists in full at that seat's session start, and the receipt prints the line to paste plus the command that starts the other agent on the row; fael never wakes an agent, and the row is read when the agent next starts or touches the file. fael claim <id> shows (held @<branch>) so a parallel agent picks something else, a signal and never a lock. Requirements and decisions written once reach every later agent that touches that code, and --revisit resurfaces a row when it is due. Its behavior rules: writing costs no extra turn (the agent runs fael add in the same message as its next tool call, or ends a reply with fael decision, issue or note lines that fael files without stopping the turn); reading and searching bring nothing, because rows wait for the edit, so a sub-agent with empty context gets the memory its brief left out at the file it edits; and rows are pushed per file once per context window (re-told after compaction) and cut to a token budget (800 by default) rather than dumped as notes. Rows retire once the code absorbs them (git owns what changed; fael keeps only what git cannot say), and fael stats and fael report show exactly what was put into context (handed over against acted on, retired at touch, handoffs picked up, across agents), under the standing line that fael never claims what it cannot measure. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our written handoffs (chief-of-staff packets, EM intent, spec and plan, vault notes) are addressed to tasks, while fael addresses memory to files, where the next seat actually looks. The pack says three mechanisms carry over even without adoption: push on edit only, with no summary stuffed in before the agent says what it will do (the README's critique of summary memory is that it averages away the one row that mattered); a claim as a signal, not a lock, for parallel worktrees; and retire-when-absorbed plus measured pickup, so the ledger cannot rot into stale notes that still get injected. The pack places it beside kept pair-mailbox (seat-to-seat delivery) and the vault (durable decisions), at the in-repo, per-file layer neither covers. We already have: handoffs that pass ownership, not transcripts, through a machine-readable packet, the artifact carrying the detail and the packet the state (#handoff-packet); intent.md, spec.md and plan.md kept next to the code with git history as the audit trail (one SDK repo keeps them in the vault or local-only), and review fix passes that append a short record to plan.md instead of silently rewriting it (#em-loop); every coding stage filing vault notes so the next agent inherits state (#coding); recall that greps the notes' one-line summaries, written with the exact names a later search would use (a file path among them), and opens only the notes that apply (#memory-loop); two clocks, with fast-changing facts re-fetched live before any action or claim rather than remembered (#memory-rules); a byte ceiling on the policy files every agent reads before every task, because every task pays the full read (#resident-budget); and the rule that a count in a receipt, Decision or Lab card names how it was counted and over what (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial of file-scoped notes, decisions and issues in one active repo, written in the same turn as the work, pushed only when that file is edited, within an 800-token budget and re-told after compaction; parallel-worktree coordination by claim as a signal (held @<branch>), never a lock; and rows that retire when the code absorbs them, with fael-stats-style pickup accounting (handed over against acted on, the across-agents count) as required reporting, so an unmeasured memory claim is not accepted. The pack frames it as a one-repo trial with stats reported weekly, removing the ledger as the rollback and the vault untouched; note that its rows retire automatically, whereas our memory loop deletes durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves the specific items (#memory-loop). Caveats: young, created 2026-09-24; the pickup metrics are the author's definitions until our trial reproduces them; per-file push needs tuning so hot files do not become a new context tax; fael never wakes an agent, so delivery waits for the next start or touch and urgent handoffs still need the chief-of-staff packet; MIT, 1 star; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
