entries.title: conspectus: read-only, evidence-ranked map of agent sessions, tmux panes and worktrees
entries.why: Rust CLI and library (version 0.1.0, a pre-release; a zero-copy snapshot format and an XDG cache layout) that builds one provider-neutral map of the agent work on a machine: it locates agent sessions across multiple CLIs, terminal multiplexers (tmux, zellij), git repositories, worktrees, branches and forge pull requests, records plausible relationships as evidence and resolves them into a typed graph of 10 node kinds (agent session, mux session, repo, checkout, branch, workspace, fork, forge PR, pin, runtime process) and 22 typed relations. The graph is sparse by default: an orphan session or an unlinked tmux pane is valid data, never an error. Evidence first, resolution second: discovery never guesses; a plausible relationship is a candidate link with provenance (declared, strongly discovered, discovered, convention, cached), a confidence score and freshness, and resolvers select the preferred link while keeping the losing candidates, so an ambiguity stays visible as data (a ⚠ glyph and score breakdowns) instead of collapsing silently. Attribution follows six ranks without touching the agents: (1) a link declared in configuration; (2) a session the harness reported, or a pane process with the transcript open (/proc, lsof); (3) the harness's internal state or logs, read-only; (4) the harness process running in the pane, found by a process-tree walk; (5) the pane's launch command (argv) naming the session; (6) the pane's working directory matching the session. Pins are sessions that outlive processes: logical sessions declared by name and directory, whose compaction, resume and crash lineage is tracked so that a single command reconnects to the latest active conversation rather than spawning a fresh, disjoint session. Bounded mutation envelope: strictly read-only by default; it never types into a live agent pane and never writes harness-owned state. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our Mac fleet runs several long-running sessions across tmux panes, and tracking which pane runs which conversation, branch or task takes a manual grep. Per the pack, kept pctl covers message delivery while this covers session-to-multiplexer-to-git attribution, and its attribution rule (never type into a live pane to ask for a session id; walk the process tree and inspect open file descriptors) and its pins that outlive processes across compaction solve session tracking without intrusive instrumentation; the pack counts it, with pctl and agent-perch, as holding the tmux and session-viewer lane. We already have: every long Mac CLI run launched through a tmux wrapper with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) whose on-stale action resumes the same session, each tool's session id reused per PR or slice (#launch); the rule that a stale run resumes only after the old agent's process is confirmed gone, because killing a stale tmux session does not prove the old agent stopped, enforced since 2026-10-20 12:16 PT by the ownership guard: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead, and a session launched before the install has no ownership record, so on a stall it is parked, never killed (#watchdog-resume-safety); in the same entry, tmux-agent-status's lsof-to-rollout matching for one coding CLI listed as not adopted (#watchdog-resume-safety); the EM bot's */15 heartbeat, which reads the kick ledger before inventorying tmux and PRs (#em-loop), and an 08:06 PT pickup check that cross-checks the ledger against tmux and PRs (#coding-em-kicks); the 10-11 lesson in which a run's tmux session vanished while its agent kept running, so the queue's loop ended and the stall was found by a manual check, and the 10-15 lesson in which the watchdog re-ran an idle catch-up collect cold twice, a new conversation each time (#mac-run-lessons); and report-only checks that read state and write a report but never kill, block, restart or edit anything, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only run of its graph generation on local repository checkouts that tests process-tree attribution without typing into any pane; then the six-rank attribution model and the pin lineage logic carried into our tmux status checks; and the pack's playbook line: attribute sessions by evidence, not by typing into panes: resolve process trees and open file descriptors, keep ambiguities visible as data, and track session lineage across restarts. The pack's stop condition: attribution relies on typing into panes or fails to tell concurrent tmux sessions apart. Its open-file rank would revisit the lsof matching the playbook lists as not adopted; adopting that rank, scheduling the tool, or using its graph in a resume decision would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: version 0.1.0 is a pre-release; the six ranks, the node kinds and the provenance classes are the author's design and have not been tried against our seats or their session files; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-08-01, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Command-silence watchdog: warns on 90 s of output silence, not on total run time
entries.why: Command watchdog, a Node.js extension for one coding agent, that warns when a command stops producing output, with silence as the primary detection signal. Its doctrine, per the README: the host agent's bash tool has no default timeout and judges success only by exit code, so the worst case, a process that is alive but already broken, never produces a failure signal; 90 seconds of silence is a real signal, while a command having run for 90 seconds is not. Streaming awareness against wall-clock duration: while output keeps flowing (a 6-minute build that logs continuously, for example) it never warns; tools that do not stream (read, write, grep, ls) use wall-clock thresholds, 180 s for a warning and 600 s for critical; known-slow commands such as docker build or cargo build raise the thresholds to 300 s and 600 s; interactive commands (vim, less, git rebase -i) are skipped entirely; and while the agent waits on human input (a permission dialog, a selector) the clock freezes, so the wait is not treated as a hang. Safe by construction: the default is pure observation (mode observe), and it never kills a process or aborts a turn without an explicit opt-in (guard or yolo); it never overrides built-in tools, never rewrites commands and never modifies tool input. The author reports 82 test cases plus a live check of RPC event order. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, its silence rule would let our watchdogs trigger earlier on genuine hangs (90 s of silence, for example) while legitimate 10-minute compilation jobs still finish undisturbed. We already have: a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) attached to every long Mac CLI run, with streaming output required and an on-stale action that resumes the same session (#launch); in the controls inventory, a log silent past 540 s with no watchdog STALE action counted as a fail, and the launch standard itself a convention that nothing blocks (#controls-inventory); an EM heartbeat every 15 minutes across live agent tasks (stretched from every 5 minutes on 2026-09-21), which does not replace the ~540 s watchdog, since both apply (#em-loop); named long-CLI failure modes (crash, hang, stall, api-error), each to leave a machine-readable heartbeat that says whether the run finished and what killed it, with loop patterns kept distinct from the stale-only watchdog and that watchdog not fleet-replaced without Haiyuan's ask (#exception-first); the 10-15 lesson in which the watchdog's on-stale action re-ran a catch-up collect cold twice while the collect sat idle waiting up to 15 minutes on a background task, each run ending with a SUCCESS result and no pack, and the 10-11 lesson in which a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); and a count of stale kills, 2 of 266 watchdog marker logs from 2026-10-02 to 10-08 (#watchdog-resume-safety). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): its 90 s silence rule carried into our watchdog's logic, observe mode first, and evaluated on slow compilation tasks; and the pack's playbook line: silence is the watchdog signal, not elapsed runtime: warn when streaming output freezes for 90 seconds, but never interrupt a long job that is actively logging. Our watchdog's trigger is already silence, a run log silent past 540 s (#controls-inventory), so the new parts would be three proposed improvements, none approved: (1) command-level observation, with silence measured on each command's own output, not only on the run's log as a whole; (2) a pause for human input distinguished from a hang on stdin: the extension skips interactive commands and freezes its clock while the agent waits on a permission dialog or selector, and the pack's example of a genuine hang is a process that hung on stdin 10 seconds into a turn; and (3) the threshold evaluated, 90 s of silence against our ~540 s, on those slow compilation tasks. The pack's stop condition: false alerts fire during continuous streaming output. Any change to the watchdog's logic, thresholds or on-stale action would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it is an extension for a coding agent that is not one of our seats (#roster), so what could transfer is the rule, not the extension; its thresholds are the author's defaults, not tuned on our runs; the 82 test cases and the event-order check are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 2 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-16; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: trace: temporal-logic monitors over tool-call sequences, plus a signed audit certificate
entries.why: Interpretable, CPU-only runtime guardrail (Python 3.9 or newer; Tsetlin logic plus finite-trace linear temporal logic, LTL) that wraps an agent's tool calls and emits a cryptographic session certificate that can be verified independently. Its finding: memoryless per-call filters fail on multi-step temporal attacks; in slow-roll exfiltration every individual export call looks benign while the sequence violates policy (count_le(export, 2, 50)), and the author reports an attack success rate of 1.000 for per-call filters against 0.000 for TRACE, with false-positive rates of 0.048 or less. Three components: (1) a content guard, a Tsetlin machine that flags prompt injection and jailbreaks with human-readable Boolean clauses (IF ignore AND previous → UNSAFE), running in about 107 µs; (2) a behaviour guard, online, bounded-memory finite-trace LTL monitors (Always, Never, BoundedCount, Response, Precedence) that evaluate temporal policies at O(1) per step (4.9 µs / 322 B); (3) a certificate ledger, a hash-chained, HMAC-signed, Merkle-rooted audit log that an external party re-verifies offline without calling a model. It normalizes tool calls from multiple frontier providers into one canonical schema. Documented limitation: F1 of 0.827–0.967 in distribution collapsed to 0.209 under cross-dataset shift, taken as evidence that static syntactic rules need temporal and behavioural anchoring. The author reports 40 passing unit tests. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness contracts set strict policies (no secrets in notes, read-before-write, the three-round fix ceiling, human approval before external action), and compliance is checked today by post-hoc reviews or prompt instructions. Per the pack, TRACE is a lightweight formal monitor (4.9 µs, CPU-only) for multi-step sequence invariants, such as the pack's examples precedence("authorize", "deploy") and bounded_count("retry", 3, window=10), that outputs a verifiable certificate, and it shows that safety constraints can be deterministic and mathematically verified without adding model latency. We already have: run limits that long fires inherit (50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend, 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval) and a stop on abnormal input volume, as policy in charters and skills, with a wrapper that enforces them outside the agent loop still a Lab follow-up, not live (#run-limits); the retry ceiling (transient failures ≤2, schema repair once, three failed correction rounds, then escalate), with unknown outcomes parked rather than auto-retried (#retry-ceiling); RED actions, among them send or publish, spend, merge, delete non-junk, permissions and production, always asked of Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), and an approval re-checked against the approved item and current authority right before the action runs (#approval-recheck); a pre-tool gate in our decision layer that, before a high-risk tool-server or shell mutation, returns allow, ask or deny and scores destructive, exfiltration and cost risk (playbook §13, gates table); untrusted content treated as data, never instructions, as policy text that nothing enforces (#untrusted-content); one receipt line per routine run (time, routine, outcome, note), written even when nothing happened (#receipt-line), and weekly receipts, because a bot can summarize its history but should not be its only judge (#kill-review); and, in the controls inventory, the run-limit and fix-round, approval, no-secrets and untrusted-content rows all marked manual, with fix rounds counted by hand, no enforcing wrapper live and no secret scan in the note tool (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): an offline trial that evaluates its CPU-only finite-trace rules (BoundedCount, Precedence) on recorded tool trajectories and verifies the HMAC-signed Merkle ledger; then finite-trace checks prototyped on our EM loop's transitions, with session certificates verified offline; and the pack's playbook line: certify sequences, not just individual calls: use lightweight finite-trace temporal logic to catch multi-step attacks that memoryless filters miss, and sign the audit ledger for offline verification. The pack's stop condition: an evaluation step exceeds 1 ms or requires neural-network dependencies. Putting it in front of live tool calls, letting any of its verdicts block a step, or holding the signing key its ledger needs (keys never go in the vault or hub HTML, #extend) would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the attack success rates, false-positive rates, F1 figures, timings and test count are the author's, read in the README, not re-run, and none is ours; its cross-provider normalization has not been tried on our seats' tool calls; the pack's spawn-ok probe shows python3 runs on this Mac, but its version was not checked against 3.9; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-18, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: deadweight: static audit of the config an agent silently ignores, with a count ratchet
entries.why: Deterministic static auditor for coding-agent configuration (Python 3.9 or newer, no dependencies, no network; CI on Linux, macOS and Windows) that opens on the failure it targets: 'Your coding agent ignores part of its configuration, and it doesn't tell you.' Two of the real findings in its README: an agent definition missing its name is dropped at load, and calling it gives 'Agent type not found' and nothing else; and a deny rule Bash(git:* push --force) matches nothing, because :* is recognised only at the end of a pattern, so the colon is literal. Its check families: permission rules that never apply and settings in the wrong file; agents and skills that never load, and hooks that never fire (unknown events, matchers that match nothing, scripts that are gone); dead links, rule globs that match no file and dead path anchors; text loaded on every turn that nothing uses (the standing instruction file's size, the always-loaded and skill-listing budgets); skills whose descriptions are close enough to steal each other's triggers; eval suites that cannot fail or cannot run; credentials in files every clone receives; and instruction files placed where their tool does not look. The part the pack would take is the ratchet: --set-floor freezes today's counts and --check-floor fails if they rose, and the floor records the auditor's fingerprint and refuses to compare counts taken by a different auditor version, because 'A measurement with no floor is one people learn to ignore: the numbers move, nobody owns the direction, and a year later every step looked reasonable.' Notices are never omitted, since '0 errors, 0 warnings' is not the whole answer while notices exist, and exemptions cannot silence the checks that audit the overlay or the ratchet itself. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it is the missing read-side check on the surface our fleet installer writes: the shared skill copies carry no manifest and no checksum, and today's own failure is an instance, one seat's copy of the Lab source-collect skill being malformed, with no YAML frontmatter, so that seat cannot load it by name while the prompt path still works: a skill that never loads, and nothing warns. Per the pack, kept agent-docs-lint (2026-10-11) checks dead references in docs and kept catstack checks symlink and prune install integrity, but neither checks whether a hook fires, whether a skill loads or whether a permission rule can ever match. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the homes of the coding CLIs, and the shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills); in the controls inventory, that wiring marked enforced on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract in the vault and one copy whose checksum matches, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, both sizes recorded in the daily digest (#resident-budget); cited vault paths that must resolve, the Monday card sync checking those cited in the fleet contract and the role cards, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check); a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input (#check-can-fail); and a Monday kill review that asks of each routine whether it ran, whether its output was right and whether anyone would miss it (#kill-review). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): its read-only audit on a copy of the vault and one project skill mirror, today's counts frozen with --set-floor and --check-floor run in the weekly kill review, a weekly check first and its plugin only if the static pass finds real load failures; and the pack's playbook line: audit what the agent ignores: a permission rule that never matches, a skill that never loads and a hook that never fires are invisible failures; freeze today's count and fail the week if it rises. The pack's stop condition: if the static pass cannot see the skill homes of the two seats it was not built for and finds nothing actionable in the mirrors, keep only the check taxonomy and the ratchet. Running it on the live vault or in a live seat's home, installing its plugin, adding the floor check to the kill review, or taking up its hooks-that-never-fire family, which comes close to the declared-versus-effective hook loading the playbook lists as not adopted (#resident-budget), would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the findings and check families are the author's, read in the README, and none was run on our files; it is shaped for three coding tools, among them the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, and not for two of our other seats, so it will not see their skill homes unless pointed at them; its opt-in semantic layer sends configuration to a model; its measure flag opens a session of that harness without the workspace-trust dialog, running the project's hooks and tool servers, and the pack puts that flag out of bounds; MIT, 2 stars, created 2026-09-22, pushed 2026-10-22 21:01 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: tripwires: each guard rule carries its incident, its test and a weekly verdict
entries.why: Pre-tool-use guardrail (Node 18.17 or newer, no dependencies, ships CI; hooks for two coding CLIs plus a generic stdin and stdout protocol) that attaches four things to every rule: 'the incident that caused it, the fix the agent should use instead, a test built from the real command, and a weekly report that tells you whether the rule is helping or hurting.' The denial teaches the fix: tripwires try "pkill -f node" prints DENY, the rule id, why the command is wrong ('killing by image name hits every process with that name, including the shell this session runs in'), the exact alternative (list, pick a PID, kill that PID) and the override syntax, and 'The agent reads that text instead of running the command.' The author lists eleven rules, each born from a dated incident with a count of how often it happened first, among them kill-by-name (three times in a month), secret-file-read (six times in five weeks) and deploy-burst (419 deploys and 6,285 credits in a month). Overrides are loud: TRIPWIRES_ALLOW=<rule-id> counts only at the head of a command, and tripwires allow <id> --because "<the person's own words>" takes a one-shot pass and writes those words into the log; in the README's words, 'Nothing stops an agent from typing a reason itself; what this gives you is that every pass is in the report with its justification.' The weekly report gives each rule its denied, overridden, error and session counts and p50 latency, one example line per day and a blank verdict to fill in (helped, hurt, no effect or confounded, with evidence); a hurt verdict backed by three wrong denials means narrowing the rule and adding the real command to its tests. Its parsing rule is 'Data is not code': a heredoc written to a file is not a command, echoing a test runner's name is not an invocation and a trailing comment is not an override; and since rules are code, a rules file cloned in a repo needs an explicit trust step first. It fails open when its engine throws, because a broken guard must not kill the session. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our never-again list and our hook rules are conclusions without their tests, and the Monday kill review gives no rule a verdict; this supplies the missing lifecycle: date, incident and count, the real denied command as the test, the legitimate neighbours as pass cases, and a weekly helped, hurt or no-effect verdict with evidence. It also forces an explicit fail-open or fail-closed choice, which, per the pack, our fleet has never written down per hook; and per the pack, kept everyhook (2026-10-19) translates one hook source across agents and kept rollcage-guard and bouncer supply the guard mechanism, while this is rule governance, each rule's maintenance record. We already have: the repeat-lesson rule, under which a correction already filed twice or more becomes a proposed fix where the rule is applied, such as a checker or hook spec, after the never-again list came to hold 18 near-identical paragraphs (#repeat-lesson); a byte ceiling on that list (81,155 B), past which a new line means compressing or demoting another (#resident-budget); wrong or outdated lessons put on a prune list and deleted only item by item once Haiyuan approves (#memory-loop); a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input (#check-can-fail); the completion-claim rule, prose with no hook installed, any hook for it a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); a pre-tool gate in our decision layer that returns allow, ask or deny before a high-risk tool-server or shell mutation, a verdict below its confidence floor going to the chief-of-staff route (playbook §13, gates table); and the Monday kill review, which judges each routine, not each rule, against the kill condition its prompt states before it runs (#kill-review, #kill-condition). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the four-field rule record and the weekly report, for never-again entries and for the two or three hook rules that, per the pack, actually deny; a trial of the tool on one seat's coding CLI only, installed with its dry-run flag, with no rule that denies reads except of credential files; and the pack's playbook line: every rule carries its incident, its test, and a weekly verdict: the denial must teach the fix, and a rule nobody has judged in a month is a rule to retire. The pack's stop condition: any rule that denies a read, other than of a credential file, or adds more than 600 ms to a normal call is not adopted. Installing it on a live seat, letting any of its rules deny a call, or setting a hook to fail open or closed would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and any hook change is Tier 3 under the review-depth rule (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the eleven incidents and their counts are the author's, and so is the 200–600 ms start-up cost per matched tool call, measured on a loaded Windows laptop, not on our Mac; it hooks only two coding CLIs, both run by our seats (#roster); its rules are executable code and need a trust step; failing open suits an interactive seat but is the wrong default for CI unless flipped; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-21, pushed 2026-10-22; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-memory: warn-only linter for memory rot, from oversized handoffs to stale facts
entries.why: Plain-file, per-project memory for coding agents (bash plus jq, on macOS and Linux; a session-start hook and a linter) that the author uses daily across about 30 projects, built around a linter for rot. The author's failure list is the useful part: append-only growth (one handoff reached 56 KB with 35 dated sections, and one index had 31 current-state bullets, injected into every session); stale state, such as being logged out of a site or waiting on something, read as current by the next agent; the same rule in four places, drifted apart; no mechanical check, so everything depended on agents behaving; a hook that forced writes, later removed: 'A Stop hook blocked the agent whenever files changed but memory didn't. Agents complied by appending something every turn.'; and two parallel memories that can contradict each other. Its linter, memory-check, warns and never blocks, on: a handoff over 6 KB, older than 7 days or with 3 or more dated headings (the append-only smell); a waiting or running section 2 or more days old; an index over 8 KB or with more than 3 current-state bullets; index links that point nowhere, and records the index does not list; records without a status, or with a superseded-by pointer to a missing file; and facts stamped as of a date older than 3 days. Limits are environment variables, and the warnings surface at session start beside the index and the handoff, with the handoff's age. Its design rules are the transferable part: the handoff is a snapshot, not a log, rewritten whole while git keeps history; one home per fact, standing rules in the agent's standing instruction file and project knowledge in memory; volatile state kept out or date-stamped for the linter; decisions superseded, not deleted; 'check mechanically, nudge softly'; and no forced writes, since staleness is caught at the next session start instead of by making every turn write something. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the vault is our durable memory, and its handoffs and packs are append-only artifacts: every day adds a pack, the shared Today note grows, and a waiting-on line sits in notes long after the wait ended. Per the pack, kept Agentic Vault Skeleton (2026-10-14) covers layout, kept vault-memory (2026-10-20) covers recall and the kept memory-loop card covers write discipline, but none has numeric rot thresholds or a 'snapshot, not log' rule; and the negative result is as valuable as the linter: a stop hook that forces a memory write every turn teaches agents to append noise, a direct warning for any rule to write a learning note after every task that we are tempted to tighten. We already have: the vault as the team's long-term memory, a context repo rather than a chat log, whose daily consolidation merges lessons that say the same thing (#vault); the memory loop: write only what is new, open every note with a one-line summary that recall greps, keep the post-task note mandatory, keep Decision notes as the audit trail with a superseded one pointed to by its replacement, and delete durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves each item, policy text that nothing enforces (#memory-loop); fast-clock facts (Mac connected, a PR tip, quota, CI state) re-fetched live before any action or claim rather than remembered, and a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on each new Decision note and standing-rule memory (#memory-rules); for shared user memory, one dated, sourced line per fact, a replaced fact forgotten in the same turn (an exception to the rule that deleting non-junk needs Haiyuan, but only in the drafter's reading, which Haiyuan has not yet ruled on; every other forget waits for Haiyuan's approval) and a Monday prune pass that only proposes (#shared-memory-admission); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, both sizes recorded in the daily digest (#resident-budget); and cited vault paths that must resolve, the Monday card sync checking those in the fleet contract and the role cards, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): only its linter, about one shell script, ported onto a copy of the vault with the 6 KB, 7-day and 3-heading defaults and kept warn-only for two weeks before any hook blocks, measuring how many handoffs trip; not its stop hook, and not its installer's import into the live global configuration; and the pack's playbook line: lint the memory, not just the code: cap the handoff and index by size and age, rewrite the handoff as a snapshot, and never force a write every turn. The pack's stop condition: if it fires on most packs and nobody reads the warnings, retire it, and add no blocking hook. Running it on the live vault, scheduling it, adding any hook, or rewriting notes as snapshots, while our deletes of durable lessons stay item by item with Haiyuan's approval (#memory-loop), would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the failure list and the thresholds are the author's, from the author's own projects, not tuned on our vault; its installer edits the global standing instruction files of two coding CLIs between markers, a live-config write that must not run unattended; warnings never block, so it works only if someone reads them at session start; MIT, 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-21 20:21 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: mac-dev-janitor: kills a runaway process group, then leaves the agent a note why
entries.why: Two parts for a Mac that runs many coding agents (Python for the watchdog, shell for the cleanup, two launchd agents, no sudo). Its resource watchdog samples ps every 10 s and groups processes by process group, since 'Coding agents run each shell command in its own group, so one group is one command.'; it sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL 10 s later, to a group with a physical footprint of 8 GB or more (or the largest group, at 1.5 GB or more, after 30 s of memory pressure), a group that used 3 or more cores while the machine was at least 85% busy for 2 minutes, a group that used 0.9 cores or more for 20 minutes straight, or an orphaned dev tool older than 3 hours (its parent died, no terminal). Eligibility is narrow: only descendants of a list of known coding agents, or a known dev tool started from a terminal or orphaned; never touched are any group containing an agent or a terminal emulator, app bundles (editors and their language servers), system binaries and launchd jobs, and shells, so the shell returns exit 143 to the agent instead of vanishing. The note is the mechanism: every kill is logged as JSON lines, notified and printed to the process's terminal, and an overload, runaway or memory kill is also appended to a kills file in the user's state folder, with the command's working directory and an instruction for the agent; a bundled agent-rules file tells the agent to read that file and run a smaller command instead of retrying the same one, and the installer can append it to the agent's standing instruction file. A daily cleanup runs at 20:00 through a launchd agent: git worktree remove, never forced, for one tool's settled or orphaned worktrees, a purge of node_modules, dist and target folders in projects untouched for 7 days, a cache clean, a container prune and deletion of unavailable simulators, with a dry-run flag to preview it. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it aims at host survival rather than agent logic, while our watchdogs judge the run log, not the machine; two rules transfer: kill the process group, not the process, since a test runner's workers hide behind an idle root; and 'a kill without a note is a retry', since an agent that sees only exit 143 runs the same command again, so the kills file plus the agent rule is what breaks the loop. Per the pack, kept whystuck and watchdog-kit watch the agent's progress, while this watches the host's memory, load and orphan set, and it gives the 15 GB floor a concrete pre-launch cleanup path with a dry run. We already have: long launches held while the Mac has less than 15 GB free, a floor since 2026-10-11 (#launch) that only one queue's disk gate enforces, the shared launcher having no disk check (#controls-inventory); the Mac run lessons: launches held at 12–14 GB until space was freed, a nearly full disk the likely cause of an app-level disconnect on 10-11, and the 10-15 exec wedge, in which newly started programs hung before running (#mac-run-lessons); after any Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes that must exit 0 before any launch, relaunch or resume (#spawn-ok); a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) on every long run, whose on-stale action resumes the same session (#launch), and, since 2026-10-20 12:16 PT, an ownership guard that refuses a restart unless the old process is proven dead, since killing a stale tmux session does not prove the old agent stopped (#watchdog-resume-safety); named long-CLI failure modes (crash, hang, stall, api-error), each to leave a machine-readable heartbeat saying whether the run finished and what killed it (#exception-first); unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked, not auto-retried (#retry-ceiling); Mac checks that only report, never kill, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks); and deleting non-junk on the RED list, always asked of Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the watchdog in dry-run mode for one week on this Mac, then only its memory and runaway rules, at a 12 GB group threshold and a 20-minute runaway window; its cleanup's dry run ported as the pre-launch disk check, with the container prune left off; and the pack's playbook line: kill the process group, and leave the agent a note: an idle root hides its workers; exit 143 without a reason is just a retry. The pack's kill condition: any kill of an agent or terminal group, any container volume prune, or a false kill on a legitimate long build kills the trial. Letting it kill anything on this Mac, scheduling either part, appending its rule to a seat's standing instruction file, or any delete beyond a dry run would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it was created on the day of the pack, and its README states no test suite, so per the pack it is a well-described script, not a proven tool; its container cleanup (a system prune and a volume prune, both with the all flag) deletes every unused volume, a data risk the pack says not to enable; its purge deletes dependency folders in repos untouched for 7 days, rebuildable but slow to recover; cleanup needs Full Disk Access for a wrapper app; its thresholds are the author's defaults, and the pack calls the 8 GB default high for a 24 GB machine already near the free-space floor, yet its trial uses a 12 GB group threshold; MIT, 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-22; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: skill-trigger-bench: listing-budget lint plus a trigger eval with a negative control
entries.why: Two checks for the 'I wrote a skill and the agent never uses it' failure (Python 3.10 or newer, no dependencies, an optional YAML parser; CI for lint and skills; a composite CI action). Its lint runs offline over a folder of skill directories, or one skill: the skill format's spec rules, frontmatter among them, plus a description that 'says what it does, never when to use it', a description budget (all descriptions together against a --budget default of about 15,000 characters), trigger overlap (a TF-IDF cosine of 0.35 or more, listing the shared terms), duplicate names, a body over 500 lines and missing references; output in JSON, SARIF or a code host's CI format, a suggest mode that never edits, and exit 1 on errors. The number that matters is the author's own run over a personal skill folder of the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs: 43 skills whose descriptions total 22,086 characters against the ~15,000 budget, so 'roughly 13 of them may never be shown to the model.' Per the README, descriptions share a listing budget, and once enough skills are installed some are 'silently never offered'; it also prints two real collisions between near-namesake skills, at cosine 0.56 and 0.50. Its eval measures whether a skill is reached for: each prompt is one run of that harness in its headless stream mode, in a fresh temporary project with only the chosen skills and project-only settings, so the user's own skills do not leak in, tools that could change anything turned off and turns capped at 2; only an explicit call of the harness's skill tool naming the skill counts, not reading the skill file by hand. It reports a trigger rate and a false-trigger rate and exits 1 below a minimum trigger rate (default 0.8) or above a maximum false-trigger rate (default 0.2); a dry run prints the prompts with no calls, and a prompt file supplies 10 or more should-trigger and should-not-trigger cases. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we install the shared skills into six homes with no description budget and no trigger check, and have already paid for the class twice: one seat's copy of the Lab source-collect skill is malformed, with no YAML frontmatter, so it cannot be loaded by name, which the lint's frontmatter rule would flag; and the skill catalog in a live session is large enough that the description budget is plausibly blown. Per the pack, kept deadweight (2026-10-22) audits whether configuration is ignored, kept skillwharf (2026-10-01) counts which skills fired, from logs, after the fact, and kept catstack, driftproof, Harness Wrangler and the blind A/B skill-eval card measure whether a skill improves output; none measures whether a skill is chosen, with a negative control, and the false-trigger side is the part we lack: a skill that fires on everything scores a perfect trigger rate and is useless. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the coding CLIs' homes, and the shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced in the controls inventory on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract and one matching checksum, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list (#resident-budget), folded from kept coding-agent-guardrails (2026-09-28), which per the pack caps always-on rules, not the skill listing; the promotion-gate rule that moves a routine or skill up the autonomy ladder only with three clean runs, a rollback tried once and a complete receipt (#promotion-gate), and a replay regression check before a skill or prompt change is promoted, marked proposed in that inventory because its replay set of our own failures is not built yet (#replay-check, #replay-set); and, as policy text only, a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input, and a check that examined nothing reporting a gap, never a pass (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the offline lint first, with no model, on a copy of each of the six shared skill homes, recording the total description characters and the overlaps; then the eval's dry run; then a 10+10 prompt eval on one shared skill with a negative control; the budget treated as a per-harness measurement, not the tool's 15,000-character constant; and the pack's playbook line: a skill that is never listed cannot be chosen: measure the listing budget and the trigger rate, and ship a negative control so a skill that fires on everything cannot pass. The pack's stop condition: if the lint cannot see the frontmatter in two of our seats' skill homes, or the budget does not reproduce a hidden skill, keep only the budget measurement; if the false-trigger control cannot be met, do not gate on it. Spending on its model-backed eval, since spend is on the RED list that always goes to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), running either check on a live skill home or in a live seat instead of a copy, adding one to a routine or a CI gate, or gating any skill on its trigger or false-trigger rate would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the 43 skills, the 22,086 characters, the hidden-skill estimate and the collisions are the author's run, not ours; the ~15,000-character budget is community-measured, per the README's sources, not an official constant, and two of our seats may differ or not list skills the same way; the overlap rule is lexical, catching the obvious collisions and missing paraphrase; the eval spends money per prompt, and 4 prompts is 'far too few', the README asking for 10 or more per side; its runners for two other coding CLIs are heuristic and, as the README says, not run live; installing it from git is a code install, for a throwaway environment, not a live seat; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-09, pushed 2026-10-23 07:13 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.whatItIs: Two checks for skills an agent never uses: an offline lint, including whether all skill descriptions fit the space the agent lists them in, and a paid test of how often a skill is picked when it should and shouldn't be.

In the author's run, roughly 13 of 43 skills may never be shown; a trial on copies is only proposed, not installed.

entries.title: lcc: compaction that keeps spans verbatim, stashes what it drops and explains every cut
entries.why: Local context compiler (Python 3.11 or newer; a CLI, a tool server and a plugin for the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs; on the Python package index as local-context-compiler, since the package named lcc there is unrelated) whose compaction does not summarize: kept spans stay byte-identical, removed tool outputs go to a content-addressed stash, and recall re-hashes on read; the placeholder left in a cut's place states lines and size, not tokens, plus the recall id. Every pass writes a relevance-compaction-1.2 JSON report, and its explain command, given the report and the source, gives the reason for every kept or dropped block. Providers are local by default: a rules provider with lossless, recoverable and stashed modes, a local trained ranker and a mechanical provider; an optional remote ranking provider is opt-in only, needs a key and can be switched off by an environment variable, because 'having a key is not consent to send context off-machine.' Its plugin refuses a pass below a 25% gain and keeps the harness's built-in summary, and the report exposes the provider used and whether the pass degraded. The evidence is the author's, not ours: one real session of 193 messages and 75 tool calls went from 57,083 to 28,807 tokens (−49.5%), 43 of 43 messages byte for byte and 33 tool outputs removed, each one recallable; across 266 long sessions the median cut was 22.7% (middle half 15–32%, best 65%), with 0 messages lost; a pre-registered 172-request test found an agent answering from the stashed context plus recall did as well as full context on file recall (+0.006, 95% CI −0.023 to +0.034) with 36.6% fewer tokens, calling recall for 90% of questions about removed content; and a summary of the same sessions in the style of a built-in compact command got 73% of exact values right, against 98% for full or verbatim context. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our long runs, packs and stream transcripts are lossy at the boundary: kept compaction-stress-lab (2026-10-11) measured how lossy, one compaction keeping about 1 in 5 exact tool-printed details, but it is a study, not a mechanism; kept context-guard (2026-09-30) caps growth and forces a handoff; kept agent-memory (2026-10-22) lints memory rot; kept ai-coding-gateway trims noisy tool output; and none makes a cut inspectable and reversible. Per the pack, the transferable rule is one we keep asserting in prose, that a lossy step must leave a receipt, what was dropped and why, and a hash-checked way back, with 'structural PASS is not answer quality' as the honest boundary the README itself draws; and none of it is applied here: no per-drop receipt, no recall id, no re-hash on read and no rule that keeps the summary when the gain is under 25%. We already have: streaming output required on every long Mac CLI run, one seat having no stream-json mode and a compressed session file (#launch), a convention that nothing blocks (#controls-inventory); the vault as the team's long-term memory, a context repo rather than a chat log (#vault); done receipts whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted, a manual control in that inventory (#done-receipt), and, as policy text only, a check that examined nothing reporting a gap, never a pass, while a passing check says what it examined (#check-can-fail); the promotion-gate rule that a routine or skill moves up the autonomy ladder only with a complete receipt, each run's record of what it did, its inputs, outputs and side effects, beside three clean runs and a rollback tried once (#promotion-gate); the 10-11 run-log lesson, not a Decision lock, in which a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); and an ai-coding-gateway-style trim of noisy tool output listed among the Lab follow-ups as new practice, not installed (playbook §11, Lab follow-ups). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pattern plus a measure-only trial: its measure-session command run offline on one stored transcript, counts only, and its explain command on a compacted copy; the receipt fields, dropped span ids, hash, recall id and the degraded flag, adopted for pack truncation; no install of its compaction plugin until the seat's harness version supports function hooks and we have a rollback; and the pack's playbook line: a cut you cannot inspect is a guess: keep spans verbatim, stash what you remove, and make every drop explain itself with a hash-checked way back. The pack's stop condition: if the transcripts are unreadable or the 25% floor is not met, keep only the receipt pattern, with no blocking compaction and no remote provider. Installing its plugin or tool server in a live seat, setting the early-access function-hooks flag, compacting or blocking a live session, turning on the remote ranking provider, or changing how packs are truncated would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and any hook change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the evidence numbers all come from the author's own sessions; its local trained ranker was trained on transcripts of the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, so two of our other seats are out of distribution, and plain text uses the mechanical provider; the plugin needs version 2.1.274 or later of that harness and an early-access function-hooks flag; its protection rules 'reduce, but do not rule out, lost evidence'; the optional remote ranking provider sends context off-machine and, per the pack, must stay off; an Apache-2.0 notice covers one optional integration; MIT, 15 stars, created 2026-06-19, pushed 2026-10-23 08:54 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: lcc: trims an agent's context without summarizing, and explains each cut
entries.whatItIs: A context compactor, local by default, that shrinks a coding agent's context without summarizing: kept text stays exact, removed tool outputs are stashed and can be recalled, and a report gives the reason for every kept or dropped block.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes, our long runs and packs lose detail when cut, with no record of what was dropped and no way back. A counts-only trial on one stored transcript is proposed, not approved; its reported gains are the author's own, and it is not installed.

entries.title: skillrouter: a small resident skill core, the rest of the library searched on demand
entries.why: Skill router for an agent host (Node 20 or newer; a CLI, a local tool server and a routing skill; version 0.2.0-beta.1) that splits an agent's skill library into two tiers to prevent context bloat: the core, a minimal set of frequently used skills, stays preloaded in the host's prompt, and the library, the broader collection, stays on disk and is searched on demand through two lightweight tools on its tool server, search_skills and read_skill. Its diagnostic CLI has doctor, which verifies host connectivity and tool registration, index --root over a folder of local skill directories, and search; trim --dry-run inspects which skills can be safely offloaded from the host's preloaded configuration to the on-demand library, without deleting files; and a standing routing instruction tells the agent: 'before non-trivial work, search relevant skills and read matching instructions; follow host permissions and use only skills relevant to the task.' Why it matters here: per the collection pack, kept skill-trigger-bench (2026-10-23) points to the listing-budget limit: in its author's run, 43 skills had descriptions totaling 22,086 characters against a budget of about 15,000 characters in the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, a budget that card calls community-measured, not an official constant, so roughly 13 of them may never be shown to the model. Per the pack, we install the shared skills into six homes, and every skill is preloaded, all or nothing, in each seat's skill directory, so as more skills are added the preloaded listing risks blowing the budget and hiding critical skills; this is the architectural remedy, a lean resident core kept in the prompt and the rest queried through fast local tools on demand, and none of it is applied here. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the homes of the coding CLIs, and the two shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced in the controls inventory on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract and one copy whose checksum matches, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, which covers those two files only (#resident-budget); the promotion-gate rule that moves a routine or skill up the autonomy ladder only with three clean runs, a rollback tried once and a complete receipt, a manual control in that inventory (#promotion-gate); and a replay regression check before a skill or prompt change is promoted, marked proposed there because its replay set of our own failures is not built yet (#replay-check, #replay-set). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the small resident core plus on-demand library architecture, tried first in a scratch project: its doctor command run and one skill directory indexed, search_skills and read_skill tested there, and a check of whether on-demand search frees resident context without lowering the trigger rate; and the pack's playbook line: preload the core, route the rest: keep a minimal skill core resident in the prompt and let the model retrieve specialized skills on demand via a local tool server to stay well under listing budgets. The pack's stop condition: if on-demand search adds high latency, more than 3 s per call, or the model fails to search for skills that are not preloaded, keep the skills resident. Installing its tool server or routing skill in a live seat, offloading any skill from a live seat's preloaded listing, adding its routing instruction to a seat's standing instruction file, or changing the fleet installer or the shared skill homes would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a change to the installer is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, which counts writes to shared state or across repos, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the 43 skills, the 22,086 characters and the estimate that roughly 13 skills may never be shown come from the author's run in the skill-trigger-bench card the pack cites, not ours and not this project's; per the pack, the extra tools add latency, a search and a read before the work, and the model has to recognize when to search for a skill instead of having it resident in its system prompt; version 0.2.0-beta.1 is a pre-release and needs Node 20 or newer; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-22 21:20 PT, pushed 2026-10-24 09:08 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: skillrouter: keep a few core skills loaded and look up the rest when needed
entries.whatItIs: A pre-release router that splits an agent's skills in two: a small core of often-used skills stays loaded in the prompt, and the rest stay on disk, searched and read on demand through two local tools, to keep the prompt from bloating.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes, every shared skill is preloaded in each seat, so adding skills risks overflowing the listing space and hiding some. A trial in a scratch project is only proposed; the extra search adds latency, and it is not installed.

entries.title: yardgoat: a verifier frozen by hash decides done, and a blocked task parks its question
entries.why: Task coordination engine, its 'yard engine', for coding-agent CLIs of different kinds (Python 3.10 or newer; a CLI and a task reconciler; adapters for three coding CLIs, all three run by our seats (#roster), and for a plain shell), with three formal guarantees. One owner per task: only the registered owner can dispatch or verify, and ownership is transferred explicitly and survives controller restarts. No duplicate dispatch: re-dispatching an active task returns the existing run, and an exited run must be verified before another attempt. 'A receipt, not a vibe': process exit and task verification are strictly separated, and a task passes only when its verifier command, frozen by hash at submit time, exits 0. Question parking: a worker that is blocked or needs human input writes out/BLOCKED.md, and the task parks automatically; yardgoat inbox displays the pending human questions, yardgoat answer supplies the human decision, and yardgoat reconcile, run from cron or on an event, resumes execution. Its yardgoat quick command, given a prompt and a verify command, generates a complete task card, the frozen verifier and a spec in a single command, and warm execution pools reuse agent sessions across tasks. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it implements three of what the pack calls our core harness locks: code decides done, where the agent's self-report is untrusted and only a deterministic verifier script frozen up front decides success; support for our mixed seats, through adapters for the coding CLIs they run; and the human gate, since, per the pack, the session gate needs Haiyuan's approval before destructive actions or ambiguous choices, and writing BLOCKED.md to park a task until an answer arrives replaces busy-waiting and keeps the agent from guessing. Per the pack, none of it is applied: we use custom shell wrappers and manual prompt dispatches. We already have: code decides done, under which a task is done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, while agent self-reports and the decision layer's completion check are advisory only (#code-decides-done); a completion claim that counts only if the session record backs it, the EM and each reviewer scanning the diff for test tampering, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), all three under completion validation, a manual control in the controls inventory (#controls-inventory). We also have exclusive ownership of a run's output, enforced since 2026-10-20 by an ownership guard that gives each launch an attempt ID, lets only the current attempt publish and refuses a restart unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety); unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked for Haiyuan or the EM, not auto-retried (#retry-ceiling), and anything that cannot be undone in under a minute parked and asked, under the reversibility tiers (#gyr-authority); a kick ledger whose rows go from posted to launched to PR open or done, or to blocked with a note (#coding-em-kicks); and a decision queue, one file for the irreversible items and judgment calls waiting on Haiyuan, each with the question, options and our recommendation, an item unanswered for 3 or more days re-raised once (#decision-queue). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the frozen verifier hash requirement and the out/BLOCKED.md question-parking convention in our EM dispatchers, and a trial of yardgoat quick for reproducible test receipts, first run as yardgoat quick with a frozen verifier command on a simple task, with BLOCKED.md parking tested in yardgoat inbox; and the pack's playbook line: code decides done, questions park: verify task completion with a verifier command frozen by hash at submit time, and park blocked runs in a structured file rather than letting the agent guess. The pack's stop condition: if frozen verifiers cannot accommodate dynamic test output, or worker session locks fail on restart, adopt the BLOCKED.md convention only. Running it on a live seat or repository, routing a real kick through it, scheduling yardgoat reconcile from cron, or changing how the EM dispatches, verifies or parks work would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a wrapper, cron or routine change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: git-warden: a pre-receive push wall with green, yellow and red verdicts and quarantine
entries.why: External push guard for autonomous coding agents (Go 1.24 or newer; two binaries, push-guard and backup-guard) that intercepts git push before commits reach the remote, so that only checked SHAs get through: its pre-receive hook reads the remote refs fresh with git ls-remote, never trusting the agent's local tracking state, isolates the new objects in quarantine and evaluates its rules, a secret scan among them, keeping push.jsonl as the audit trail and red pushes as bundles under pending/. Its gate has three colors: green is an atomic fast-forward push to the real remote with the guard's own credentials (git push --porcelain --atomic), never with --force; yellow is a rejection returned with exact file:line:reason diagnostics, so the agent can self-repair without human intervention; and red is a hard block that needs human approval ('rejected: waiting for a human'), the commits quarantined in a git bundle and the owner notified by a command or a webhook. A backup guard adds append-only lineage tracking (git-everref) against branch deletion and history rewrites. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, client-side git hooks can be skipped with --no-verify or modified by an agent with shell access, while a pre-receive guard is a boundary the agent cannot bypass, which isolates unreviewed commits, runs secret scanning and cleanly implements our green, yellow and red ladder, enforcing what the pack calls our standing push rules: no exit while waiting, hermetic-first push and never pushing without review. Per the pack, none of it is applied: we rely on client-side checks and review gates before a push. We already have: an EM loop in which the implementer commits, pushes and opens the PR without waiting for reviewers, blind review starting only once a PR exists (#em-loop), and merge by Haiyuan only (#coding); reviews that count only with a verdict line on the current head SHA (#review-verdict-line); no exit while waiting, under which an agent does not end a turn waiting on background CI or live jobs with a dirty tree, but foregrounds to a durable exit or pushes hermetic-first and runs a second pass (#coding), a manual control whose wrapper gates for a dirty tree or an unchanged HEAD are hand-written per kick (#controls-inventory); an always-on play that keeps advisory policy in skills and must-hold rules in hooks, no secrets in a diff and no push to main among them (#em-loop); a test-tamper scan that also looks for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repo's hooks, policy text only (#check-can-fail); an approval that covers the item as approved, the PR head SHA included, re-checked right before the RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck); and, for vault notes, a manual control with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a study of its pre-receive quarantine and its yellow and red feedback as a pattern for a remote push gate, evaluated against a prior push-gate Lab card the pack cites (history not confirmed here); a first trial on a test bare repository with its pre-receive hook, verifying that atomic pushes are accepted and that unreviewed pushes and force-pushes are rejected with yellow or red diagnostics; and the pack's playbook line: guard the remote at the door: place a pre-receive push wall between agents and Git remotes so force-pushes, secrets, and unreviewed commits are quarantined before hitting upstream. The pack's stop condition: if the bare intermediary repository creates excessive push latency or authentication complexity with the code host's remotes, keep the local push gates. Putting it in front of a real remote, handing it push credentials, a permissions change on the RED list (#gyr-authority), letting it notify anyone by command or webhook, running its backup guard on a real repository, or changing any push path or gate would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a hook or wrapper change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: continuity: a session ledger detects handoffs made stale by its own work
entries.why: Session continuity built around a record and a thin handoff, with a shared engine for a coding CLI and a second coding CLI. Its checkpoint command writes the current session's handoff JSON without ending the session: working directory, session id, git.head at checkpoint, branch, next action, open loops and uncommitted files from a per-session ledger of touched paths. It does not commit, merge or push; a handoff that fails lint is still written with the failure reported. The documented stop hook writes a skeleton without blocking if no handoff exists, but prompts an update and blocks that stop if this session's own work made an existing handoff stale. Staleness comes from touched files and session-owned commits in the ledger, rather than file age. After compaction it restores this session's handoff with a reminder to revalidate against the record; its context guard warns at 50% when usage data is available. Its improve-harness command routes a concrete mistake to its narrowest owning rule, skill, agent definition or memory, and independently reports over-limit instruction files and exact or near-duplicate rules, naming both files and line ranges. Both passes are report-only even unattended; agreed edits stay uncommitted. One CLI adapter refuses checklist and checkpoint writers from headless sessions and subagents; sweep is watch-only with no scheduler. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our handoff packet has no check that it still describes the tree, and the interrupted curate runs required manual state checks before resuming. The playbook confirms those checks and interruptions (#mac-run-lessons, #idempotent-resume). Per the pack, agent-role-contracts rejects stale handoffs at offline preflight and agent-memory lints stale facts after the fact; the proposed delta is staleness computed from this session's own edits at stop, plus a commit the next session can compare. The report-only instruction checks also give the repeat-lesson rule a mechanical proposal path; these checks are not applied here, per the pack. We already have: handoff packet v1, whose artifact holds the detail and whose packet holds the state, with a completeness check that is report-only, shadow only and never blocks, box-side and unverified from the Mac (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory), rather than only the hand-followed format the pack describes; idempotent resume, which checks live state before each step that writes and skips completed steps, a manual step documented by the curate checks (#idempotent-resume, #mac-run-lessons); repeat lessons routed to a proposed diff at the owning source, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory), inside daily consolidation, marked enforced in the inventory but box-side and unverified (#vault, #controls-inventory); a resident-policy byte ceiling whose fold size gates are report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); and replay before a skill or prompt promotion, proposed because the replay set is not built (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the two checks, rather than the plugin: add git.head and a touched-paths ledger to handoff packet v1 so the next session compares rather than trusts, and propose a report-only duplicate/over-limit pass over loaded instruction files. First trial checkpoint and pickup in one scratch repo before any live hook. The pack places the instruction pass in weekly consolidation; our consolidation is daily (#vault), while the Monday sync has the manual kill review (#kill-review, #controls-inventory). The pack's summary line for continuity: a handoff this session invalidated cannot be left standing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit criterion is supplied for this KEEP; the stated boundary is a scratch-repo trial before a live hook. The playbook requires a pre-written routine kill condition, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion, changing the handoff packet or consolidation, installing a live stop or restore hook, or allowing automatic instruction edits would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). A tmux-launched run needs an explicit kill path and a blocked-stop beat-log line. Shell-driven edits need explicit ledger registration and can go untracked; without a user-owned record destination the handoff points to nothing. The playbook now has report-only skill lint (#skills); that checks skills, not this proposed pass over loaded instruction files. entries.title: agent-ops-kit: only explicit IDLE skips a cycle; a broken precheck is WORK
entries.why: Four small pieces for headless scheduled loops, extracted by the author from a system running 119 background jobs (Python 3.10 or newer, standard library only, plus portable shell). Jobs touch a heartbeat file on success; missing or stale heartbeats become append-only alerts.jsonl findings, fingerprint-deduplicated to one unresolved alert per problem: 'Log, don't page.' A deterministic precheck prints IDLE or WORK: <reason>; only explicit IDLE may skip a cycle, while errors fail open into WORK, a corrupt config counts as enabled and a crashing precheck counts as work. Its wrapper orders kill switch, single-instance lock, precheck gate and wallclock budget with hard kill. The repair skill validates, classifies, fixes only if provably safe, verifies, rolls back on doubt and leaves one digest line, with shadow mode, at most 2 attempts, protected paths and human escalation. The author's 7-day audit of one real hourly loop found about 95% no-op runs and about $231 per week in API-equivalent spend for zero changes. This is one author's audit of one loop, not a benchmark and not our number. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, collect and curate decide nothing new by judgment, and a failed, rate-limited or stale lookup can look like a quiet hour. Only explicit IDLE being allowed to skip makes the negative-claim rule part of control flow. Per the pack, overlapping collect runs and runs that never return motivate the single-instance lock and wallclock kill, and the deduplicated alert file could feed the existing sole missed-slot detector rather than create another one. Those are proposed controls, not measured savings or existing per-routine heartbeat files here. We already have: negative claims requiring a successful, fresh lookup and a failed fetch reported as gap:, never zero or quiet, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); routine receipt lines even when nothing happened, checked in the manual weekly receipts review (#receipt-line, #kill-review, #controls-inventory), rather than this project's success heartbeat file per routine; the sole Field Brief missed-slot detector, marked enforced but box-side and unverified (#controls-inventory); long-run tmux, streaming and stale-log watchdog use, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), alongside exclusive run-output ownership and refusal to restart until the old process is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); and run limits stated in policy, with runtime enforcement still a follow-up, not live (#run-limits). The existing shadow launch decision is manual, logs only and never blocks; fixed schedules skip it and always run (#worth-running-scope, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the IDLE / WORK: contract in collect and curate prompts backed by a real precheck command for a new live-Lab updatedAt, a new pack file or a new push since the last run; non-zero exit means WORK. Add a heartbeat touch on success and one alerts.jsonl consumer; put the single-instance lock and wallclock kill in the launcher. The pack's summary line for agent-ops-kit: only a deterministic check may say IDLE; a broken check is WORK. The pack's stop/kill condition: no trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; the wrapper's kill switch and wallclock hard kill are mechanisms, not a stated trial criterion. The playbook requires a pre-written routine kill condition, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion and the budget for fail-open work, changing a fixed schedule to permit IDLE skips, choosing the new-material check, wiring heartbeat alerts into a routine, or changing launcher locks or kills would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A launcher or routine change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers); spend is a manual Haiyuan approval gate (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory). Caveats: the 119 jobs and the 7-day, about 95% and about $231 per week figures are the author's, not ours; errors deliberately consume tokens by becoming WORK and need a budget line. New material is ours to define and that check can be wrong; protected paths are prompt-enforced, not sandboxed, and state paths are operator-trusted with no containment. The standard-library scripts would still be code we own. The pack says curate is at 16:30 PT; the playbook says 16:45 PT (#usage). Skipping scheduled cycles would change the playbook's fixed-schedule always-run rule (#worth-running-scope), not merely replace its shadow decision. entries.title: dsh-skill-pack-security: a caller-enforced pre-install scan with named misses
entries.why: Deterministic pre-install supply-chain scan for the open-source agent harness one of our seats runs, with 8 audit skills and a zero-dependency plugin_vet provider. Given an owner/repo or local package, it checks license evidence, a lockfile dependency tree with optional external vulnerability checks and their source annotated, immutable 40-hex commit refs in install manifests and workflow actions, malicious patterns in lifecycle scripts, exfiltration domains and encoded payloads, and data-responsibility findings such as ungated sensitive listeners, undisclosed outbound endpoints and instruction-override payloads embedded in shipped text. A five-dimension risk card scores license, source, dependencies, build scripts and maintenance from 0–100 and folds them into PASS / WARN / FAIL. The default warn policy is non-blocking; deny still depends on the caller wiring the verdict into its installer or CI. It does not intercept the host's plugin-add command. The author's own benchmark in the repo's benchmark/RESULTS.md has 38 samples, 20 malicious and 18 benign, over three pattern checks: micro precision 1.000, recall 0.850, F1 0.919 and FPR 0.000. Per-class recall is 1.000 for install scripts, 0.667 for network exfiltration and 0.833 for obfuscation. The three named misses are the messaging-service webhook samples ne-pos-03 and ne-pos-04, where receiver-domain comparison against the bare URL host fails, and the inline-base64-via-variable sample ob-pos-01. These checks catch shapes, not intent and have no vulnerability database. The benchmark is the author's, not ours; optional dependency vulnerability checks do not change that limitation of the pattern checks. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, shared skills are copied into six homes and third-party plugins and skills run with the seat's file access; the existing adjacent cards address pinned-content identity, install integrity and hook behavior, rather than package safety. Per the pack, no pre-install scan, third-party commit-pin rule or license/SBOM check is applied in those homes. The pack cites kept skill-trigger-bench (2026-10-23) for listing-budget pressure; a measurement of our shared skill homes is history not confirmed here. The refreshed playbook already documents skill lint, so that existing report-only check must be distinguished from the proposed supply-chain scan (#skills). We already have: a fleet installer wiring the vault contract and shared skills into CLI homes and project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced on link and checksum evidence checked on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); skill lint adopted today for frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets, report-only, never editing skills, rerun in Monday sync with alerts only for a rising count or a new error (#skills); untrusted material treated as data rather than instructions, policy text only, classified manual in the inventory (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory); the open-source harness pinned to 0.2.1-rc.2 or newer on the 0.2.1 line, enforced by the updater skipping it (#controls-inventory); and skill promotion requiring three clean runs, rollback tried and complete receipts, manual, with the replay check still proposed because the set is not built (#promotion-gate, #replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): trial plugin_vet in a throwaway profile against one real third-party plugin and one local skill pack, recording the PASS/WARN/FAIL card before deciding whether it belongs in the fleet installer; verify the provider's own card from a clean profile, since installing the scanner is itself a plugin install. Separately propose immutable 40-hex pinning and instruction-override-payload checks for packages shipped into a seat. Keep the 8 skills out of a live seat for now; use one language edition in one root. The pack's summary line for the package scanner: scan the package before it enters the seat — and print the misses.
