entries.title: dsh-ctx-budget: estimate resident context and check contract paths
entries.why: Static-context auditor for the open-source agent harness one of our seats runs (Python 3.10 or newer, standard library only). Its six layers cover standing-rule bytes, memory counts and token estimates, skill counts and frontmatter characters, tool entries with schema tokens reported as null, session count and disk use, and a read-only knowledge database, plus an optional cost layer. Read-only by default, it requires --apply for writes, with backups and atomic replacement, and makes no network or model calls. Its capabilities command checks backticked paths, exiting 1 for broken paths, and looks up single-segment commands without treating an unknown command as broken. Its probe command reads plain or compressed session logs and request tool arrays: cold starts with zero cache-read tokens estimate static context as the first prompt minus the first user message; warm sessions return null rather than a guess. The memory commands audit or archive entries, while skills can compress long descriptions and write backups on --apply. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the collector found one shared contract file reached through two symlinks and loaded twice in the same session; these are collection-time measurements, not re-verified here. Its contract spot check counted 61 backticked path-like tokens, 45 resolving directly and 16 false alarms for a naive run: 7 templates or model identifiers and 9 home-prefixed paths that all existed after expansion, leaving 0 dead pointers. The proposed path check therefore needs home-directory expansion and template skipping. Per the pack, session probing could supply a per-seat static-context usage line; the updated playbook already has resident-policy byte ceilings and a cited-path rule (#resident-budget, #pointer-check), so the delta is per-request estimates and a calibrated report, not inventing those controls. We already have: resident-policy byte ceilings for the two files every agent reads before a task, with daily consolidation recording both sizes and fold size gates classified report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); cited vault paths required to resolve before a pointer is written, with Monday sync checking contract and role-card paths while skipping placeholders, a manual step described by the rule with the upstream lint tool not installed (#pointer-check); adopted skill-description budget lint and a one-time static config audit, both report-only, neither a measured per-request context cost (#skills); and negative claims requiring a successful fresh lookup, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory). The blanket pack claims of no resident-context measurement and no contract path check overstate the gap: byte checks and the path-check rule already exist, while per-request static-context estimates are not documented on these playbook surfaces. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): run ctxbudget baseline and probe --since 7d read-only on the existing seat, recording an estimate in the usage dashboard as a per-seat static-context line; run capabilities on a copy of the shared contract file after teaching it home-directory expansion and template skipping. Propose a report-only weekly step until it has run clean twice, alongside the existing Monday path-check rule. Keep skills --apply off shared homes and do not use memory-archive until the tool has more than a day of use. The pack's summary line for the context auditor: measure what the seat pays before its first token; a dangling pointer must exit non-zero. Here that number is an estimate, not billing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; two clean runs before considering a blocker and more than a day of use before the named writes are staging boundaries, not a kill threshold. The playbook's pre-written routine kill condition is policy text only, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion, installing the CLI or plugin in a live seat, adding the dashboard line or weekly step, making path findings block work, or allowing description rewrites or memory archiving would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine, hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: one author, no external validation, created and pushed within about 20 minutes on 2026-10-25; Chinese-first docs with an English summary. The memory half is inert on this Mac because its memory directory did not exist at collection time; the collector counted only 2 skills and 21 session directories, a small sample, not re-verified here. The duplicate-load and path counts above are also collector measurements at collection time, not new checks or author benchmarks. Token counts are estimates, not billing, using 2 characters per token for CJK and 3.5 for English; truncated tool descriptions make the tool surface a lower bound, the system prompt is never persisted, and warm sessions yield no static number. Description rewrites affect shared files. The plugin bundle is a third-party install: per the pack, scan it through the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate first, and installing the scanner is itself an install. entries.title: memcap: heavy commands wait for memory across sessions; light work never queues
entries.why: Shared memory budget and admission queue for every session of two coding CLIs on one Mac, both run by our seats (#roster), plus an always-on background watchdog that retires what agents leave behind (Mac only; shell plus standard-library Python 3.9 or newer). Pre-tool-use hooks see each shell command first: searches, reads and git status never touch the queue; only commands with positive evidence of heavy work (builds, test runners, simulators, containers) go through admission, and unrecognized syntax alone does not queue. A queued command starts only when memory pressure allows it (red always blocks; unknown pressure admits nothing), its reservation fits the physical headroom and the previous start has settled; reservations follow measured peaks of earlier identical workloads, incomplete measurements never shrink an estimate, and missing ones are reported as unknown, never as healthy zeros. Cleanup runs through one kill choke point in narrow tiers (orphaned dev servers past a 300 s age gate, over-budget dev servers, idle simulators and browsers), re-verifying identity before TERM and again before KILL; agent CLIs and its own ancestry are never targets, MC_DRY_RUN=1 previews, and memcap off pauses everything. Each watchdog pass stamps a heartbeat, and past the stale threshold its status prints 'MEMCAP IS PROBABLY NOT RUNNING', added after the author's machine ran 28 hours without enforcement while its status still printed a budget; the founding incident was a 24 GB Mac hard-shut-down with 388 orphaned dev servers and 20.3 GB of swap in use. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, several seats run on this Mac at once, each starting test suites or builds on its own, and the fleet has had the neighboring failures (exec wedge, disk at 99 %, stalls). Per the pack, kept command-silence-watchdog (2026-10-21) asks whether a command went quiet, kept whystuck (2026-10-18) asks why it hung, kept watchdog-kit (2026-10-18) escalates ignored alerts and kept agent-ops-kit (2026-10-25) gates whether a cycle fires; none of those four rations the machine across sessions, so two seats can pass all of them and still push the Mac into swap together. The transferable rules, per the pack: light work must be provably light or it queues; an unknown measurement admits nothing, our own gap: rule in control flow; and a watchdog that cannot prove it ran must say so in its status line. We already have: long launches held while the Mac has less than 15 GB free (#launch), a manual control that only one queue's disk gate enforces (#controls-inventory), a disk floor, not a memory budget per command; after Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes, a failed one meaning nothing is launched and a gap is recorded (#spawn-ok), run by hand, report-only in the inventory (#controls-inventory); long runs in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), with a restart refused unless the old process is proven dead, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); failed lookups reported as gap:, never as zero, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); and two report-only Mac checks, installed with no schedule, one reporting the freshness of run logs, packs and receipt lines (#report-only-checks, #controls-inventory). The playbook's heartbeats are run-level (#launch, #em-loop); the nearest local evidence for the pack's watchdog-liveness rule is a run lesson in which a queue's watch loop ended with its tmux session and the stall was found by a manual check (#mac-run-lessons). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial in observe mode only, adopting the admission rules before any kill tier. Install it in a scratch window, run its init step but leave enforcement paused (memcap off) and garbage collection at the default GC_MODE=observe, then use its status and classify commands and MC_DRY_RUN=1 for a week to see what it would queue or retire here. Unpausing is discussed only after that dry-run log has been read, and no tier may kill until the protected-process list is extended. The pack's summary line for memcap: heavy work waits for memory across all sessions; light work never touches the queue; an unknown measurement admits nothing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is that a plain text search must never enter the queue, which the author treats as a reportable defect ('lightweight-queued'). The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the package, its background watchdog or its hooks in any seat, even paused; unpausing enforcement; arming any cleanup tier; extending its protected-process list; reconciling its queue wait with our launcher; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, launcher or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: hooks cover the two coding CLIs only; per the pack, four other seats get no admission, and its built-in agent list, extendable through a variable, does not name those seats, so kill classification must be verified before any tier is armed. It is a process-killing, always-on service whose README history includes killing a deliberately daemonized server (a parent pid of 1 is also what nohup produces) and shutting down a simulator a live run was driving (fixed, and logged). Admission is not an operating-system memory limit, so running work can overshoot between samples; hook timeouts fail open in the host, and our run lessons record tool-use hooks stalling two runs (#mac-run-lessons); managed commands default to a 24-hour queue wait and background execution, which per the pack must be reconciled with our launcher walls; the playbook's nearest timing control is the stale-log watchdog at about 540 s (#launch). A package plus hooks in live seats is a third-party install: per the pack, the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate card applies, itself a Lab proposal, and one coding CLI's hook trust stays user-approved. The 388 orphans, 24 GB, 20.3 GB of swap and 28 hours are the author's figures, not ours; the pack's spawn-ok and free-disk readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. One maintainer and fast version churn (versions 0.16 to 0.18 in one README); MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-08-13 22:49 PT, pushed 2026-10-27 22:18 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. entries.title: docgraph: two separate doc graphs flag unlinked, placeless and untracked docs
entries.why: Pre-push or CI gate, a Go binary, over a repository's agent-facing documentation graph, the docs an agent navigates by grep and links rather than the rendered site, built as two graphs that are never unioned: the content graph (findability: prose links plus inline-code path mentions), where orphans flags a tracked doc with no inbound content edge, and the metadata graph (placement: frontmatter links: edges such as part-of or depends-on), where disconnected flags a frontmattered doc with no doc-to-doc edge, edges to covered code not counting. Whole-state checks add broken links, untracked markdown (a forgotten git add), frontmatter well-formedness with a required type, edge targets and cycles, and leaks, a scan of tracked content against a machine-local, never-committed TOML file of deny terms with no hidden built-ins: no config means no rules, a warning and a no-op scan, stated rather than hidden. Its doc-drift stop hook (exit 2, once per finding) checks the session's diff for a dangling reference (a symbol's definition removed while a doc still names it), anchored value drift (a constant's numeric value changed while a doc names the constant and shows the old literal) and covers drift (code changed, its covering doc untouched); suppression lives only in config or flags, and no inline markers are ever read. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the vault is an agent-facing doc graph, measured at collection time to be a git work tree, so the tool's tracked-file scope applies, and seats navigate it by grep plus path mentions. Per the pack, kept agnix (2026-10-26) checks that a doc or skill file is syntactically valid for its host, the 2026-10-26 context-auditor card checks that backticked paths exist and kept continuity (2026-10-25) flags duplicate or over-limit instruction files, but none of the cards it names checks graph position: a Hunt note nobody links to is invisible to the next seat, a Decision with frontmatter but no edges has no place in the structure, and an untracked pack file is one git clean from gone. Per the pack, anchored value drift is the second new mechanism: our docs name constants next to their values (ports, budgets, model ids, thresholds), and nothing notices when a value moves; link health is otherwise checked by eye during curate. We already have: cited vault paths that must resolve before a pointer is written, the Monday card sync checking those cited in the fleet contract and the role cards, a manual rule for which the playbook took only the dead-reference idea from the agent-docs-lint Lab card, whose lint tool is not installed (#pointer-check), so broken cited paths are already checked by hand, more than the pack's by-eye reading; recall that greps each note's one-line summary line, written with the exact names a later search would use, policy text only (#memory-loop), so a note docgraph would call an orphan can still be found by search here; a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on new Decision notes, with no checker named (#memory-rules), the nearest thing to declared placement; a same-day sweep of every statement of an old model or seat assignment, with no checker named (#model-change-sweep), the nearest thing to value-drift control, for model and seat names only; skill lint that checks skill frontmatter, report-only (#skills); and a manual no-secrets rule for notes, with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the two-graph report and the untracked check first, with no push gating yet. Run docgraph report-only against a copy of one vault subtree, or a scratch repository seeded from it, with --skip frontmatter,leaks on the first pass, and read the orphan, disconnected and untracked counts before deciding what a clean state would even mean here. The stop-hook mode and any pre-push blocking come only after the whole-state report has run clean, or been consciously scoped, twice. The pack's summary line for docgraph: findable ≠ placed: audit both doc graphs, plus untracked markdown, before trusting the vault's shape. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is to add an unlinked markdown file and a doc naming a deleted symbol and confirm that both fire. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running it on the live vault rather than a copy, conforming vault notes to its frontmatter model, wiring its stop hook into any seat, letting any check block a push, treating its leaks scan as a secret gate, scheduling it, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, pre-push gate, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the default doc model requires a type frontmatter block on every doc except the README, a flood on the vault, and the README's own advice (conform hand-curated corpora, exclude only derived ones, never skip a check repository-wide) implies a real conforming project, not a flag day; leaks is local-only by design, since CI and fresh clones have no rules and scan nothing, so it cannot be the fleet's secret gate; the value check is not proximity-checked, so over-reporting on common numbers such as 30 or 211 is expected; a missing binary fails closed as a push gate, blocking unrelated pushes on machines without Go; and installing the binary and wiring a stop hook is a third-party install under the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate card, per the pack, itself a Lab proposal. The git work tree is a collection-time measurement, not re-checked here, and our orphan, disconnected and untracked counts are unknown until a trial runs. entries.title: custodiet: a blocking rule needs a signed law, cases both ways and killed mutations
entries.why: Stop-hook governance gate for one coding CLI (zero-dependency JavaScript on Node 20 or newer; 30 rules, 28 engine and 2 built-in) that judges a turn by its tool-call record, not by what the assistant said: rules read assistant text and tool-call inputs, never tool outputs, so reading a file that mentions git commit is not committing. Its completion rules have the familiar shape; the load-bearing half, per the pack, is how the gate governs itself. Every blocking rule carries a law: anchor to a human-signed clause plus positive and negative cases, and anchors are verified at load time in the production hook, not only in CI, so a rule with no source cannot load. Each rule ships at least 2 break-the-predicate mutations that its fixtures must kill before it may ship; the author records that when this acceptance went live, 40 of 97 existing mutations survived the old suite. Every alarm enters a denominator ledger and claimed false positives are booked with reasons (the author's machine on 2026-10-11: 205 of 2,223 rule hits, 9.2 %, self-claimed); missed detections cannot be measured, so the report prints RECALL=UNKNOWN. The ledgers carry per-row hash chains, known defects carry batch expiry dates, missing required input means UNKNOWN and blocks (fail-closed), and a block cap degrades to a notice so the hook cannot loop forever. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the completion-claim lane is the Lab's most crowded (gatehouse, proof, claimcheck, cliffhanger, kept yardgoat (2026-10-24), and rationguard as a 2026-10-26 runner-up), and what no card covers is discipline for the gates themselves: kept cheat-drill (2026-10-14) attacks hooks from outside with 39 known cheat moves, while custodiet is the inside view, where a rule earns the right to block with a signed source, examples both ways and mutations its own tests must kill, and its error rate is a ledger with the unknown printed. Per the pack, our fleet keeps adding hook rules (an install script, stop hooks, prompt gates) with no equivalent acceptance bar, so a rule that fires wrongly is found by a seat getting stuck, the cry-wolf failure the pack says our locks warn about. We already have: a new check, such as a wrapper gate or a checker script, run once against a deliberately broken input (a mutant or a planted bad line, for example) and seen to fail before it counts toward done, and a check that examined nothing reported as a gap, never a pass, policy text only (#check-can-fail), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); beside it, a rule-record reference format asking for evidence, a reproducer and a dated verdict with its owner, and for a proposed check a proof record with healthy, incident or planted-bad, and empty inputs (#check-can-fail), so cases both ways are already the documented shape; a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, never a merge gate (#mutation-testing); a controls inventory that pairs each fleet-contract rule with what enforces it, from a trial table pending review (#controls-inventory), the reverse of a law: anchor; and, for the decision layer's shadow gates, a hand check of minority verdicts before a gate goes active, manual (#constant-baseline, #controls-inventory). So the pack's no-mutation-acceptance point holds for a ship gate, not for policy: one seen-to-fail broken input is already asked in policy text, while at least 2 killed mutations per rule, anchors verified at load time and a false-positive denominator are not documented on the playbook. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the rule-acceptance contract, not the gate. Copy its five-part shape (detection over structured context only, a law: anchor, a blocking flag, positive and negative cases, at least 2 mutations) as the bar for any new blocking rule in our hooks, and start a false-positive ledger for the blockers we have, printing the unknown where recall cannot be measured. A trial of the tool itself, if wanted, is its observe mode (records only, never blocks) in one scratch repository, never the copy-mode install into a live repository, which writes agent configuration files: the shared contract file, one coding CLI's standing-instruction file and its settings file. The pack's summary line for custodiet: a blocking rule needs a signed law, cases both ways, and mutations its tests must kill — or it does not load. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting the contract; its stated boundary is observe mode in one scratch repository, never the copy-mode install. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Making the contract a standing bar for new blocking rules, starting a false-positive ledger for existing blockers, installing the gate in any seat or live repository, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision; a standing rule change gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory), and a hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: its text rules recognize Chinese sentence patterns only, and the author states plainly that in an English repository they will neither false-block nor fire; judge messages are Chinese too, so the shipped rule set is largely inert for this fleet. One user's repository is the whole deployment history, and recall is unknown, though printed; the 9.2 % figure, the 40 of 97 survivors and the stop timings (median 582 ms, p90 1,575 ms over 590 stops) are the author's own ledger, not third-party audited and not ours; the false-completion papers it cites were not re-verified in the collection; it supports one coding CLI only; its hash chain's external anchor sits in the same user's home directory, so it does not resist a process running as that user; and the anchor's install-task command is for another desktop operating system only. No local measurement backs this row; what it says about our hook rules is the pack's. entries.whatItIs: A gate for one coding CLI that judges each finished turn by its record of tool calls, not by what the agent said. Each blocking rule needs a human-signed source, examples both ways, and tests that catch deliberately broken copies of the rule.
